#5393. Trump Memecoin Dinner? Investors Wait for a Miracle

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Donald Trump is preparing another exclusive dinner for his biggest memecoin supporters, but the invitation is becoming cheaper as his token continues to collapse. The TRUMP token is down almost 99% from its peak, and this time, the presidential dinner contest closed with just 130 participating wallets holding $8.6 million, despite organizers offering 185 places.

The dinner will welcome the largest holders at Trump’s Virginia golf club on November 22. The top 29 receive an additional VIP reception, while other token holders are left watching from outside.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 President Trump to host exclusive dinner for top holders of his $TRUMP crypto memecoin on Sunday.

Just last year, wealthy buyers competed for access to Trump with millions of dollars in token purchases. This time, more than 5,000 eligible holders reportedly declined to register, while one successful entrant qualified with just $518 in purchases.

The upcoming celebration offers little reason to celebrate, as holders watched millions disappear from their holdings during the competition.

The shrinking competition exposes a problem that another presidential appearance cannot easily fix. TRUMP first memecoin dinner generated considerable excitement around the token, attracting buyers who wanted proximity to Trump and exposure to his political brand. That enthusiasm has since faded alongside the price.

Trump’s family has reportedly earned at least $635 million from the memecoin through April, according to financial disclosures and reported estimates. Meanwhile, outside investors have suffered substantial losses across several Trump-linked crypto ventures.

So, what happens to everyone who bought the token but never gets an invitation?

There is no comparable VIP experience for ordinary investors who purchased during the rally and are now sitting on losses. They cannot simply exchange their depreciated holdings for access to the president.

The frustration extends beyond TRUMP. MELANIA memecoin has also suffered a dramatic collapse from its launch-era highs, weakening confidence in the wider family-branded token ecosystem. Investors who bought into the political momentum now face a difficult question about what sustains demand once the initial excitement disappears.

World Liberty Financial is another broken painting. Its WLFI governance token has fallen towards $0.045, close to its all-time low of $0.0437. A substantial retreat from its September 2025 peak near $0.33.

Its USD1 stablecoin has also seen its market cap retreat from $4.4 billion in early October to around $2.9 billion today.

These are different products with different purposes, but their declining market valuations put pressure on the Trump-linked crypto narrative.

From bad comes to worse. Justin Sun, Tron founder, was among the most prominent early supporters of World Liberty Financial and attended Trump’s inaugural memecoin dinner. His WLFI holdings were frozen by the project, prompting him to file a lawsuit against the company just a few months ago.

The concern is no longer simply if all of Trump’s linked tokens can recover.

The market environment is hardly helping speculative assets. Iran war continues to disrupt commercial shipping and keep geopolitical risk in financial markets. Renewed attacks around Riyadh and reported tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz pushed oil prices higher on Friday.

Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was struck in a Houthi attack in the latest blow in the Iran-backed Yemeni group's war with the kingdom https://t.co/5JdXw4PKS3 pic.twitter.com/xlQvZIv7ZX

Brent crude hovers at $92, while US West Texas Intermediate reached $83. Both benchmarks were nevertheless heading for another weekly decline as expectations of a global supply surplus offset renewed geopolitical concerns.

For us, the problem extends beyond oil prices. Energy disruptions can feed inflation concerns, complicate interest-rate expectations and undermine appetite for riskier investments.

Memecoins have little protection when speculative demand disappears. The political branding behind the TRUMP memecoin cannot guarantee buyers will return after the dinner, especially when holders are dealing with substantial losses.

Trump can still host another dinner and welcome his biggest memecoin supporters, but the event cannot answer the question facing thousands of ordinary holders.

#5392. How SPS North America Connects Employee Engagement to Client Experience

Brandon Hall Group awards Silver to SPS North America for "Creating Connection Across Every Workplace," recognizing its listening-led approach to employee engagement and its focus on the people who serve clients every day.

NEW YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SPS North America has received a Silver Award in Brandon Hall Group's Excellence in Action Awards in the Employee Engagement category for its submission, "Creating Connection Across Every Workplace." The recognition honors SPS's listening-led approach to building a connected culture for more than 2,900 employees working across hundreds of client locations in the United States and Canada.

Creating Connection Across Every Workplace SPS's engagement strategy combines enterprise-wide communication and recognition programs with locally driven employee experiences. Employees provide feedback through surveys, ideas, team discussions, engagement committees and ongoing conversations with leaders. That feedback informs action plans at the corporate, regional and local levels, helping SPS respond to the needs of employees across different teams and client environments.

Employee feedback has helped shape internal communications, recognition programs, peer appreciation opportunities and learning delivery. SPS also uses a coordinated multichannel communications approach to reach employees across locations, schedules and roles.

For example, employee feedback led SPS to shift most learning into modules of fewer than 15 minutes, helping teams fit professional development more easily around operational responsibilities to clients while maintaining access to learning opportunities for team members in all roles.

Engagement That Delivers Measurable Results In 2025, SPS's Employee Satisfaction Survey generated more than 600 actionable items across operations, culture and workplace experience. Employee satisfaction increased seven points, and survey participation rose from 84% in 2025 to 87% in 2026. Ninety-one percent of employees agreed that internal and external customer needs are the focus of their daily work, while 90% said they understand the purpose of their work.

The initiative also drove strong participation across SPS North America's communication, recognition and learning programs, creating more opportunities for employees to connect with colleagues, celebrate achievements and pursue professional development. In 2026, SPS also reported a client Net Promoter Score of 91 and an overall client satisfaction score of 92. These results reflect SPS's focus on both employee experience and client outcomes.

The employee and client measures reflect SPS's focus on creating connected experiences for its people and the organizations they serve. For a broader look at how workplace data can inform business outcomes, read "Turning Workplace Data into a Competitive Advantage" and "Seven Shifts Reshaping Workplace Performance".

"This award reflects the care and commitment our teams bring to creating meaningful employee experiences across every SPS workplace," said Valerie Mahoney, CHRO, SPS North America. "By listening to employees, communicating consistently, recognizing contributions and empowering local teams, we are strengthening connections and helping our people deliver exceptional experiences for our clients. We are honored to receive this recognition from Brandon Hall Group."

"The HCM Excellence Awards have become the most recognized benchmark for excellence in human capital management because organizations know they are earned, not given. Every winning program has demonstrated measurable impact, innovation, and execution through one of the industry's most rigorous evaluation processes. We are proud to recognize the organizations setting the standard for the future of work," said Mike Cooke, CEO, Brandon Hall Group.

SPS's broader service capabilities have also been recognized by industry analysts. In the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Mailroom Solutions and Services, SPS was named a Leader.

About SPS SPS is a leading technology-driven business transformation company. With our innovative Enterprise Workplace Solutions, we empower organizations to adopt modern work concepts to enhance productivity and flexibility. Our Technology Business Solutions bring together cutting-edge technology, deep vertical process expertise, and a diverse global workforce to support clients in their digital transformation journey and efficiently tackle their most complex challenges.

Headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland, SPS operates in more than 20 countries and focuses on clients in banking, insurance and health. SPS has more than 8,000 employees and is recognized with a world-class Net Promoter Score by its global client base.

We act with precision, connect people to the right information, and turn data into insights for better outcomes.

It combines independent research, proven practices from award-winning organizations, benchmarking, strategic advisory, and the collective intelligence of a global executive community to help leaders make better decisions with greater confidence.

Brandon Hall Group's Workforce Excellence Intelligence is built on evidence. By continuously studying leadership, learning, talent, human resources, artificial intelligence and the future of work, the organization identifies what drives exceptional performance and translates those insights into practical frameworks, benchmarks and guidance.

More than 10,000 organizations worldwide, including leading employers and Human Capital Management solution providers, have engaged with Brandon Hall Group through its research, advisory services, Excellence Councils, Institute, certifications and the globally recognized HCM Excellence Awards. #5391. This Pennsylvania Real Estate Brokerage Is Doubling Down for the Changing Market

A paper house, money, and hands on a laptop. The concept of buying a home on credit or for cash.

Rather than wait for the market to change, one Pennsylvania brokerage owner is taking steps to compete in the market it has today. Broker/Owner Frank Ramos runs United | Strive 212 in Wyomissing, Pennsylvania & United | Strive 212 Lehigh Valley in Allentown, Pennsylvania. United® Real Estate shares he recently renewed his brokerage affiliation agreement with the firm, continuing the decade-long collaboration to compete within his expanding footprint. Partnering is an especially important competitive strategy in a market where home sales are roughly 25% below 2019’s pre-pandemic level, nationally. One of the nation’s 10 largest brokerages in number of homes sold in 2025, United brings national-scale tools and technology to Ramos and his agents–resources afforded through United’s size and purchasing power, the company says. However, while the scale of a brokerage partner is important, for Ramos, the decision comes down to having the support, relationships and continued innovation to compete through changing market cycles amid skyrocketing prices and a home sales slump nationwide, United notes. That partnership means he can do business without raising his overhead while keeping business costs affordable for his firm’s agents. For brokerage owners across America, the current housing conditions put an even greater premium on efficiency, adaptability and support, United explains. “United gives you the support and resources of a big company, but it still feels personal and customized to your needs,” said Ramos. “You feel valued and appreciated, and you know there are people there who are ready to help you succeed. I like the direction United is going. They keep growing, innovating and rolling out new resources that support my brokerage and my agents.” United Real Estate President Rick Haase says that exchange makes the larger organization stronger. “Markets change. Great brokerage owners adapt, lead and keep finding opportunities for their people,” said Haase. “That’s what we value about Frank and his team. They know their communities, understand what their agents need and generously share what they learn with others in our network. We’re grateful Frank has chosen to continue this partnership and optimistic about what we can accomplish together.” United provides its affiliated brokerages with technology, training, marketing, recruiting resources and brokerage support designed to help owners operate efficiently and profitably through different market cycles. Ramos says the ability to learn from other broker/owners is equally valuable. “One of the best parts of United is the network of other Broker/Owners and Managers,” said Ramos. “At United’s Leadership Summit and throughout the year, I’m able to connect with people who understand the challenges we face, exchange ideas and learn what’s working in their businesses. It’s a collaborative community where people truly want to help each other succeed.” For Ramos, United says renewal ultimately comes down to preparing his brokerage for whatever comes next. “United keeps growing and offering new resources that support my brokerage and my Agents. I want to be with a company that keeps looking ahead and finding new ways to help us succeed.” For more information, visit JoinUnitedRealEstate.com.

#5390. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

#5389. Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions, where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone, president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE. “Said another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event, Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium:

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he said during the event. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:

The financial side of AI operational readiness presents a different challenge. As enterprises scale their deployments, finance teams are establishing dedicated budget lines for token consumption and evaluating which workloads can run more economically on-premises. Repetitive financial processes, for example, can use open-weight models to convert variable token expenses into more predictable fixed costs, according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell.

“It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” he told theCUBE. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Kennedy:

The growth of AI inference is changing how enterprises distribute workloads across cloud environments, data centers and edge devices. Dell’s expanded agentic AI portfolio reflects that shift, with solutions spanning desktop systems and data center infrastructure. Organizations are evaluating where to run models based on performance, data control and cost, according to Kyle Dufresne, senior vice president of sales at Dell.

“We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?’” he said during the event. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Kyle Dufresne:

Infrastructure availability presents another challenge. Demand for AI servers has strained supplies of components ranging from memory and processors to rack-level cooling, networking and power equipment, according to David Schmoock, senior vice president of global revenue operations at Dell.

“We didn’t do that collaborative planning, and now your project may have been delayed 60, 90, 120 days, which has both the cost impact and a business impact,” he told theCUBE. “I would say bring us in earlier. Allow us to do that collaboration with you. I think, at the end of the day, you get the most optimal outcome.”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with David Schmoock:

AI operational readiness is also becoming a consideration for smaller businesses that need access to GPU computing without the resources of large enterprises. Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting this underserved market, where access to AI infrastructure can be constrained by purchasing commitments and provider priorities, according to Thomas Kato, founder and chief executive officer of Comet Cloud.

“You go to [Amazon Web Services] now; they want a multiyear contract from you. They’re picking who they’re taking,” he said during the event. “To the small and medium businesses, they’re not even coming up on that scope at all to be able to have that AI. Really, that’s our focus.”

Comet Cloud is developing an alternative approach aimed at giving smaller organizations greater control over their computing environments, Kato noted.

“What we do is we put together clusters, and we’re giving clusters to a whole company. All their information, all their security, everything is within that cluster. There’s no one else tied or connected to it,” he told theCUBE.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Thomas Kato:

Alpha Compute Corp. is also building its neocloud infrastructure around data sovereignty and confidential computing requirements. The company’s sovereign-by-design approach is intended to help customers maintain control over sensitive workloads and meet data residency obligations, including those associated with European regulations, according to Tom Richer, executive vice president of Alpha Compute.

“We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” he told theCUBE. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”

Keeping GPU infrastructure operational presents a different challenge for neocloud providers. Alpha Compute provides integrated infrastructure support and ongoing managed services to address those demands, Richer noted.

“You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he said during the event. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Tom Richer:

#5388. Great Ormond Street Hospital announces first-of-its-kind agentic AI programme in an NHS hospital, in collaboration with Hyland and Amazon Web Services

Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) is collaborating with Hyland and Amazon Web Services (AWS) on a first-of-its-kind programme exploring how agentic AI could be safely developed and deployed in healthcare. The programme will establish governance frameworks and evaluate the technology's ability to automate repetitive tasks while maintaining accuracy and human oversight.

CLEVELAND, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The 15-month 'Agentic Hospital' programme, supported by NHS England funding, will develop agentic AI tools and run them alongside current manual processes to assess how the technology could best support hospital teams. Tools are being built and will be tested in real-world hospital settings through a phased approach, helping the team build on existing governance processes and evaluate operational outcomes.

The programme comes as NHS organisations continue to face significant operational and financial pressures, with staff increasingly managing growing workloads and 31% of NHS staff saying they felt burnt out because of their work in the 2025 staff survey.1

The programme is using agentic AI technology to build tools which could streamline repetitive or high friction processes, reduce administrative burden and give staff more time to focus on areas where their skills and expertise add most value.

Unlike generative AI, agentic AI goes beyond generating answers or summarising information. It can coordinate tasks and take action across workflows, operating within defined rules and safeguards, with human oversight.

Pooling expertise across NHS and industry

While agentic AI is already being used in a range of sectors, and attitudes towards AI among NHS staff are broadly positive 2, there is still much to learn about how it could be applied in healthcare safely and effectively, and where it could add most value for patients, families and staff.

Working with industry gives GOSH access to specialist expertise and technology that would be difficult and costly to develop independently, helping accelerate learning while evaluating value for the public sector. GOSH selected Hyland and AWS as their technology and infrastructure collaborators for their expertise in workflow automation, agentic AI and healthcare.

Hyland is working closely with GOSH teams to design and build the agentic AI platform, and AWS is providing cloud computing credits and technical guidance.

The programme will use Hyland's Content Innovation Cloud, built on AWS cloud, enabling agentic AI agents to securely access information needed to gather the full context of a specific task and complete it from start to finish.

The programme will use Amazon Bedrock, allowing the team to choose different AI models for different tasks, while Hyland's AI Control Tower will provide oversight and auditing of agent activity.

The team is working closely with the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and data will be managed in line with UK GDPR.

The programme will begin with administrative functions such as content management in finance. A primary focus of this phase will be building on existing governance processes to create frameworks for the rest of the programme.

Each phase will be followed by a formal review, with progress assessed against criteria including safety, accuracy, governance requirements and the ability to reduce friction in day-to-day processes. Decisions about future phases will only be made once these assessments have been completed.

Later phases may explore clinically adjacent processes carried out after a clinician has made a clinical decision, such as booking tests or appointments. The tools themselves will not make clinical decisions.

All tools developed through the programme will operate with human oversight. Human review checkpoints will ensure tasks can be reviewed or escalated by GOSH staff based on their complexity and sensitivity.

The aim is to build evidence on how agentic AI could be deployed in the NHS safely and responsibly and which areas it could deliver the greatest benefit. The programme will run until the end of October 2027, and findings will be shared across the NHS and wider health sector. If GOSH chooses to continue using agentic AI technology, a competitive procurement process will take place.

Dr Shankar Sridharan, Chief Clinical Information Officer, GOSH and National Clinical Lead for Artificial Intelligence at NHS England said: "Agentic AI represents a fundamental shift in how hospitals could operate, improving efficiency of workflows, freeing up capacity for our staff and ultimately improving care. However, the challenge is not simply making the technology work, but ensuring it can operate safely, reliably and at scale. By bringing together NHS and industry expertise, this programme aims to establish the governance, evidence of value and standards needed to realise the full potential of agentic AI across healthcare."

Jitesh S. Ghai, CEO, Hyland said: "This programme is not just about building more AI tools, we are creating a governed foundation that lets those tools actually be trusted with real work, across an entire institution, not just one department at a time. What we're building with GOSH isn't a single hospital's AI project, but a blueprint that demonstrates how agentic AI can operate safely and transparently inside one of the most complex healthcare environments in the world â we call it the Agentic Hospital."

Ash Thankey, Managing Director and General Manager, UK, Germany and International Organisations, Public Sector at Amazon Web Services, said: "We're delighted to continue to support Great Ormond Street Hospital, a long-time pioneer of digital innovation, as it now explores what agentic AI can unlock for the NHS. Using secure, scalable AWS infrastructure and advanced agentic AI tools, GOSH's teams can safely test new ways to lift the burden of routine administration to give staff more time for patients, research, and care. These cloud and AI foundations are built to scale, and what works here could go on to deliver impact right across the NHS."

About Great Ormond Street Children's Hospital NHS Foundation Trust

Great Ormond Street Hospital opened in 1852, the first in the UK to provide dedicated inpatient care for children. We exist to advance care for children and young people with rare and complex conditions, so that they can fulfil their full potential. With all our experts under one roof, we continually challenge ourselves to research and innovate and to find better, faster and kinder treatments and share this knowledge with our colleagues around the globe through The GOSH Learning Academy.

#5387. CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a company’s employees access its business applications.

Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

The company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The company’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Every AI video tool promises a finished ad; most deliver AI slop. OpenClips.AI is the first AI video generation tool built to deliver launch-ready ads, and businesses see the price of every creative before a single dollar is spent.

OpenClips' Marketing Studio holds ready-made templates and example ads organized by industry, from restaurants and real estate to online stores and apps. Nobody has to start from a blank page or learn to write prompts: a team pastes a product link or photo and picks the template that fits. OpenClips takes care of the whole creative process, from script and scenes to voice, captions and sound, so the team only decides which ad goes live.

For mobile apps and games, OpenClips now also builds playable ads for Meta, Google, Unity and AppLovin from nothing more than a Play Store link, with no game description to write and no assets to upload.

An online store pastes its product page. A restaurant uses a phone photo of the new dish. A real estate agent uploads the listing photos, and a software company starts from a few lines about the problem its product solves.

The market is full of tools; what businesses need are shortcuts. Shortcuts to a publish-ready reel, shortcuts to ready-to-ship templates, access to skills that write scroll-stopping ads and content. #5385. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

#5384. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier

We believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:

First, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer says deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical issues.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision.  At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

As well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

That said, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:

Listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Coming back to the AI inference issue. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer said: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”

This means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

For sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a new model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

In this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:

We see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

This means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

Sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

Check out the Hyperscaler Sovereign Buyers Guide – it’s the first of its kind and very comprehensive.

And do let us know if you you have any questions – we’re here to help.

#5382. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5381. Inference now drives two-thirds of AI workloads, changing where chips get deployed

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, quickly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

“We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.)

Positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company plans to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill said. “We went with commodity memory.”

That choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

“One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very quickly,” McCaskill said. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”

#5379. Hyperliquid Anthropic Volume Explodes Past $1.7B as Hong Kong Issues Warning

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hyperliquid’s Anthropic market has surged to $1.7 billion in daily trading volume, pushing the contract ahead of Ethereum on the platform. The surge comes just as Hong Kong’s financial regulator adds Hyperliquid to its suspicious virtual asset trading platform list.

The ANT perpetual contract recorded $1.727 billion in trading volume over 24 hours on November 20. This has placed it second among Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets, behind Bitcoin but ahead of Ethereum.

Open interest also climbed to $259 million as traders built substantial positions rather than simply passing through short-term trades. The figures put Hyperliquid’s Anthropic market among the exchange’s most active markets, despite tracking a company outside the traditional crypto sector.

Just a day earlier, Anthropic ranked 17th among Hyperliquid perpetual contracts by trading volume. It then climbed to second place as activity accelerated around Anthropic’s public market debut. Its $1.727 billion turnover was 1.88 times Ethereum’s trading volume during the same period. Only Bitcoin attracted more activity, recording $5.139 billion.

The shift also displays how much Hyperliquid’s trading activity now extends beyond crypto-native assets. Six of the exchange’s top ten perpetual markets by volume were linked to traditional financial assets.

These included Anthropic, the XYZ100 technology index, the S&P 500, Nvidia, a leveraged semiconductor ETF, and South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix. Together, those six contracts generated $4.269 billion in volume, accounting for 38.1% of the top ten’s combined turnover.

ANT’s market has also attracted significant leverage. The contract allows traders to speculate on Anthropic’s share price using crypto collateral, without purchasing or owning the underlying shares.

Unlike conventional stock markets, the perpetual contract continues trading around the clock. This gives traders a venue to react to developments outside Nasdaq’s regular trading hours. This flexibility has helped attract activity as traders position themselves around major developments affecting the artificial intelligence sector.

Hyperliquid has demonstrated how much demand exists for trading assets beyond traditional crypto. Bitcoin Hyper is chasing a different opportunity: bringing Bitcoin liquidity into a much larger decentralized finance ecosystem.

The project is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 powered by Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) technology. Its goal is to let BTC holders move beyond simply holding their coins, opening access to faster transactions, decentralized exchanges, staking, and other DeFi applications.

That ambition is attracting considerable presale interest. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.29 million, with its token currently priced at just $0.01368760. More than 114,000 participants have joined the presale, giving the project considerable early fundraising momentum.

Staking is another major attraction, with the project offering rewards of up to 35% APY. That gives early participants an additional incentive to accumulate HYPER before its exchange debut, although actual rewards depend on the staking terms and participation.

Time is also becoming a factor. Bitcoin Hyper has scheduled its presale conclusion for November 26, putting its anticipated launch just days away. With the token still available below two cents, the approaching deadline could intensify demand among investors looking to secure an early position.

The trading surge comes against a growing regulatory problem for Hyperliquid. Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission added Hyperliquid and Hyperliquid Hong Kong to its suspicious virtual asset trading platforms list. The regulator specifically identified the platform’s trading interface at app.hyperliquid.xyz, stating that the entity was not licensed by the SFC.

The watchdog suspects the platform of operating, holding itself out as operating, or actively marketing an unlicensed virtual asset trading platform to the Hong Kong public.

The warning puts Hyperliquid under scrutiny in one of Asia’s most important financial centers. Hong Kong has spent recent years developing a licensing framework for crypto exchanges, requiring platforms serving local investors to obtain regulatory authorization.

The SFC also warned that investors using unlicensed platforms could lose their entire investment if an operator collapses, suffers a hack, or misappropriates customer assets.

#5378. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.
