#5377. UP Fintech: Q3 Net Income Rises 16.4% QoQ, Client Assets Reach Record US$64.8 Billion

NEW YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- UP Fintech Holding Limited (Nasdaq: TIGR) ("UP Fintech" or the "Company"), announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. In the third quarter, the Company reported a revenue of US$172.6 million. Non-GAAP net income attributable to UP Fintech shareholders was US$49.9 million, up 16.4% QoQ and marking the second-highest quarterly result in the Company's history. During the quarter, the Company added 48,500 funded clients, up 48.9% QoQ and 54.1% YoY. Total funded clients increased 11.4% YoY to 1.364 million. Supported by strong net asset inflows, total client assets rose 6.7% QoQ to a record US$64.8 billion.

The Company was named one of the world's top fintech companies in the "Wealth Technology â Neobrokers" category for 2026 by CNBC and data analytics firm Statista, the second consecutive year the Company has appeared on the list.

Mr. Wu Tianhua, Founder and CEO of UP Fintech, said: "In the third quarter, we continued to advance our global growth strategy. New funded clients rose by roughly 50% both QoQ and YoY, led by Singapore and Hong Kong. Hong Kong stood out, contributing nearly US$1 billion in net asset inflowsâa new quarterly recordâwhile client assets grew more than 20% QoQ. Client assets also increased across all our international markets, underscoring the continued trust global investors place in our platform."

"We continued to broaden market access and extend trading hours, giving investors greater flexibility. Building on our 24/5 US stock trading service, we recently became one of the first online brokers globally to offer extended-hours trading in eligible US equity options. Orders are routed directly to US options exchanges, allowing clients to adjust positions and manage risk outside regular trading hours. In December, we plan to support Nasdaq's new 23/5 trading for US stocks and ETFs from day one. As market structure evolves, we will build on our 24/5 trading foundation and continue enhancing our products and execution capabilities to strengthen our position as a gateway to US markets for global investors."

Singapore market strengthens its competitive position with prestigious recognition

In Singapore, trading activity remained strong in the third quarter, further reinforcing Tiger's competitive position in the local market. New funded clients nearly doubled QoQ, while total trading volume increased 47% YoY, reflecting the rapid expansion of the local client base and growing market appeal. Across products, trading volume in US stocks, US options and Singapore stocks increased 61%, 87% and 44% YoY, respectively, demonstrating steadily rising investor participation across both global and local markets. The Company's localized offerings also performed well. Tiger BOSS Debit Card spending reached a monthly record in September, with total card spending increasing 40% YoY. During the quarter, Tiger Brokers Singapore was named "Best Personal Investment Platform" at the Euromoney Awards for Excellence 2026, recognizing its product offering, service capabilities and market impact.

Hong Kong Net Inflows Hit Quarterly Record as Client Engagement Deepens

The Company delivered strong growth in Hong Kong during the third quarter. Net asset inflows approached US$1 billion, setting a new quarterly record. Total client assets increased 20% QoQ and nearly doubled YoY, reflecting stronger asset gathering and an expanding high-value client base. Total trading volume increased 102.6% YoY, with trading accounts up 78.7%. The Company continued to enhance its Hong Kong market data offering, upgrading Level 1 real-time streaming quotes for Hong Kong equities and making them available free of charge to investors worldwide. The Company also recently hosted its flagship offline event, Tiger Investment Festival, bringing together its digital platform and offline engagement to deliver a richer client experience and deepen its connection with the local investment community.

US, Australia and New Zealand Deliver Broad-Based Growth, Deepening Local Client Trust

In the US, TradeUP delivered strong growth in client assets and funding. Net asset inflows rose 437.4% YoY, total Assets Under Custody (AUC) increased 84% YoY, and average net funding per new client grew 58.3% QoQ. Options were the main driver of trading activity, with contracts traded up 48.7% QoQ amid rising client demand.

Client engagement also strengthened across Australia and New Zealand, as more local investors used the Company's platform to access global markets. In Australia, total trading volume increased 88.8% YoY, new margin accounts grew 40.3%, and margin account AUC rose 116.1%. In New Zealand, total orders increased 28% YoY, with Australian and Hong Kong stock orders up 54.4% and 46.7%, respectively, reflecting growing demand for cross-market investing.

US Options Trading Hours Expand; Overnight Activity Up Nearly 80% YoY

In the third quarter, UP Fintech generated US$63 million in commission revenue, while interest-related income reached US$85.5 million, up 12.5% YoY. During the quarter, the Company expanded its derivatives toolkit with the launch of an Options GEX Analytics hub, bringing together gamma exposure, trading volume, open interest and Max Pain data. These tools help investors better understand market positioning, identify key price levels and make more informed trading decisions. In Hong Kong, the Company introduced a rollover feature for Hong Kong stock options*, allowing users to switch quickly between near- and longer-dated contracts and making it easier to roll longer-term positions. In Singapore, the platform introduced odd-lot trading for local equities and Fill-or-Kill (FOK) orders, lowering the barrier to higher-priced stocks and giving investors greater flexibility. The Company also launched a dedicated Daily Leverage Certificates (DLC) section, accessible from the rankings page or by searching for "DLC".

The Company's US stock overnight trading activities remained robust in the third quarter, with overnight trading DARTs up 76.9% YoY, underscoring demand for access beyond regular market hours. The Company also recently extended trading hours for selected US single-stock options**, giving clients greater flexibility to trade outside the regular session.

Despite a moderation in Hong Kong's IPO market, strong growth in the Company's retail client base drove aggregate IPO subscription amount to over HK$172 billion in Q3, up 261% YoY and reflecting growing engagement among global investors.

Wealth Management Grows as HNW Client Base Expands

Market volatility and opportunities across asset classes continued to drive demand from high-net-worth investors for diversified portfolios, yield enhancement and professional asset management. Active wealth clients with at least US$1 million in assets increased 20.4% QoQ. Structured note trading volume reached a record US$385 million, up 168% YoY and setting a new high for the second consecutive quarter. Mutual fund AUC rose 14.2% QoQ, while assets managed under the Company's Hong Kong Type 9 license increased 262.5% YoY to US$540 million.

#5376. Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

“We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller said. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”

#5375. Washington state regulator issues temporary stop on new business for Directors Mortgage

Washington’s Department of Financial Institutions issued an emergency order for Directors Mortgage to temporarily cease accepting new business in the state. Examiners said the company failed to provide requested records and showed signs it was not meeting financial obligations to employees and vendors.   AI Summary

The Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) has ordered Directors Mortgage to temporarily stop taking on new business in the state, including the origination of loans for Washington residents or for properties located in the state, citing exam interference and concerns about the company’s finances.

According to the DFI’s order, examiners who conducted an on-site review at the Oregon-based lender’s main office from Nov. 17 to Nov. 19 were not provided requested information and records. During that period, the department served a subpoena on the company’s CEO and owner to obtain the production of original books, accounts, papers, records and files.

The department also said it obtained information during the examination indicating that the company was not meeting its financial obligations to employees or third-party vendors.

“Respondent’s failure to comply with the Department’s examination authority and Respondent’s current financial condition pose a serious risk of injury to the public,” the order states.

A representative of Directors Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment.

The emergency order, signed on Friday by Brian J. Guerard, Washington DFI’s acting director, requires Directors Mortgage to deliver detailed financial information, including balance sheets and bank account data, and to fully respond to the department’s subpoena. The order also directs the company to satisfy outstanding financial obligations.

Under Washington law, companies may contest such orders in an administrative hearing. If a respondent does not seek a hearing, the order becomes permanent when DFI issues a final order.

Directors Mortgage, founded in 1998 by president and CEO Mark J. Hanna and headquartered in Oregon, has originated about $235 million in mortgages year to date, according to InGenius. The company had roughly 40 loan officers and nine active branches as of Monday, per data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System.

Washington’s DFI has been active recently regarding mortgage enforcement. Newrez recently agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement wide-ranging mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the department that it engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

Earlier this year, Washington state regulators issued a $75,000 fine and a $3,000 investigation fee against West Capital Lending, alleging multiple violations of the state’s consumer loan act. The company was accused of allowing unlicensed individuals to conduct mortgage-related activities and of failing to meet certain disclosure and reporting requirements. Per the agreement, WCL did not admit to the allegations nor any wrongdoing.

Meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group recently agreed to pay a combined $6.75 million to the New York State Department of Financial Services to resolve allegations of cybersecurity violations tied to data protection, risk assessments and incident reporting.

#5373. Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

Robotics component maker coprod Inc. announced today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

At the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the company’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

Coprod is tackling the issue wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”

The company claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The company is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the company’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the company’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

Component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

Delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, said coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.

#5372. Human review remains paramount for AI mortgage underwriting

Leaders at Incenter Diligence Solutions and SitusAMC say AI can index, extract and flag inconsistencies across mortgage documents, improving review speed. They caution that blank fields, unusual scenarios and model behavior require human validation, plus ongoing testing and QC.  AI Summary

Artificial intelligence is helping mortgage lenders and due-diligence firms review loan files and extract borrower information, but integrating AI into underwriting processes isn’t a one-and-done experience. The technology still needs human oversight, experts say, especially when loans involve unusual circumstances or require judgment beyond standard guidelines.

At Incenter Diligence Solutions, AI has accelerated document indexing and data extraction, according to president Pamela Hamrick. Technology can now sort and categorize thousands of pages of loan documents in minutes, replacing a process that once required employees to manually separate and label files.

Hamrick said that while AI can extract information from standardized mortgage documents like loan estimates and closing disclosures, borrower-provided records — including pay stubs and bank statements. — are harder to process because their formats vary.

AI, however, can identify inconsistencies across documents and summarize them for underwriters to investigate.

“The technology is identifying the questions, and the inconsistencies and the anomalies, between all of this documentation, and summarizing that for an underwriter or a reviewer … to dig deeper and make a decision about whether or not what the AI has identified is a real risk — or if it’s a minimal risk or maybe it’s no risk at all because of the particular scenario,” Hamrick said in an interview with HousingWire.

Julia Curran, senior managing director of residential AI products at SitusAMC, said the company uses AI to re-underwrite closed loans in the secondary market, checking regulatory and underwriting guidelines as well as data accuracy before loans are reviewed for securitization.

According to Curran, SitusAMC builds AI agents around processes established by human subject matter experts and tests their results against loans previously reviewed by people. She said the company runs repeated tests until the system reaches at least 95% accuracy.

But the technology still needs the human touch. Curran said the system sends blank or inconsistent fields to human reviewers, and final credit decisions require judgments that cannot be reduced to individual data points.

“A final credit decision shouldn’t be made by the machine because there’s other things to consider besides the specific data points,” Curran said.

Hamrick added: “Companies that fully rely on AI are potentially going to have misses in some other areas where a human might have been able to make a different decision.”

Curran also warned about the AI model supplying information not supported or provided by the documents submitted. She described a case in which a model supplied a solar panel number that was not included in a particular loan file. The answer was correct, but the system had apparently drawn on information from other files.

“Even though it’s right, I don’t want that answer,” Curran said. “I want to stay within the four walls of this file.”

The executives said lenders should test AI against established human processes before relying on it for underwriting.

Hamrick recommended introducing the technology in one part of the workflow at a time, comparing its results with human reviews before expanding its use. She also said lenders should prepare employees for changes by retraining them for tasks that require more human intervention.

“The best thing that we can do as leaders is look where the technology can ultimately take over, and then take the folks that are doing those roles and train them to be better at the things that require more human intervention,” she said.

Curran said quality control requires testing models across different loan types and scenarios. SitusAMC maintains a test bank of hundreds of previously reviewed loans, including purchases, refinances, adjustable-rate mortgages and loans with rate buydowns. When a model changes, the company runs its prompts against the test bank to check whether results remain consistent.

These tests add costs that lenders may overlook. Curran said companies should ask AI vendors how their systems were developed, whether subject matter experts helped establish the processes and whether ongoing regression testing is in place.

“You want the same answer every time,” Curran said. “The process of taking a non-deterministic process and making it deterministic takes a lot of time and effort.”

#5371. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5370. ABB helps scale industrial AI with world's first motor featuring built-in intelligence

ZURICH, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ABB today launched Intelleqtâ¢, the world's first low-voltage motor with intelligence integrated at the factory, designed to deliver real-time operational insights from its first rotation. Its open architecture enables customers across industries to connect motor data to their existing digital platforms while retaining full ownership of their data. By delivering equipment-level intelligence through a plug-and-play solution, Intelleqt helps companies build the data foundation needed to scale AI-driven operations.

Intelleqt arrives as industries increasingly seek to move artificial intelligence from pilot projects into core operations, with data quality and availability remaining among the main barriers to adoption. Industrial AI can deliver measurable value, but scaling its deployment remains challenging.

While 84 percent of manufacturers report benefits from artificial intelligence, only 20 percent of AI use cases have successfully scaled.1 At the same time, the equipment powering critical sectors such as data centers, water infrastructure and food production remains one of the largest untapped sources of operational intelligence.

More than 300 million motor-driven systems operate worldwide, accounting for 60 percent of industrial electricity demand2. Yet most are not connected to the digital technologies used to improve reliability, efficiency and performance. As electrification, automation and industrial AI accelerate, the $18 billion global IEC and NEMA low-voltage motor market is also positioned for further expansion.

"ABB's investment in research and development is always focused on solving real customer challenges," said Stefan Floeck, President of ABB's IEC Low Voltage Motors division. "The shift towards AI-driven operations is accelerating, yet most of the motors powering global industry do not generate data and remain invisible to the intelligence being built around them. ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is a world first that opens a new chapter in motor development, transforming motors from mechanical equipment into sources of real-time intelligence."

By turning motor data into actionable insights, ABB Intelleqt helps customers improve reliability, increase productivity and identify energy saving opportunities of 30 percent or more3. Early fault detection can reduce unplanned downtime by up to 50 percent4, helping industrial operators avoid failures costing up to $1.5 million per incident5. Factory-integrated sensing, edge computing and connectivity give customers access to these insights from day one.

ABB Intelleqt is the latest example of ABB's investment in artificial intelligence and digital technologies, bringing equipment-level intelligence to one of industry's most important and widely used assets while helping customers build the data foundation for the next generation of industrial AI.

Launched today at the SPS trade fair in Germany, ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is now entering a customer co-creation phase, working closely with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and end users to develop solutions tailored to their operational needs. A broader rollout is planned for 2027, initially focusing on markets in Europe, Japan, China and India.

ABB drives shared success with customers through innovation and customer-focused research and development. Drawing on more than 140 years of engineering expertise, ABB plans to invest 4.5 to 5.0 percent  of Group revenues in R&D to support the development of pioneering technologies such as ABB Intelleqt. In 2025, ABB invested $1.3 billion in R&D. The company has around 7,800 R&D employees across facilities in more than 30 countries on six continents, with approximately half focused on digital and software development. Since 2022, ABB's total R&D investment has increased by around 30 percent.

#5369. Post-quantum cryptography startup Q.security launches with $11.5M in funding

Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc. formally launched today with $11.5 million in new funding for a platform designed to take enterprises from discovery through to completion of their quantum-safe migrations.

Founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program. The company argues that security teams need business context to decide which cryptographic findings to address first, since the time and resources available for the work are limited.

At the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications. Findings from the cryptographic inventory are tied back to that map, with the highest-risk assets put at the front of the queue.

Teams are said to be able to investigate exposure and work through remediation using a conversational artificial intelligence interface. Through integrations with existing cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, the platform drives fixes to completion using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing and automation.

Once a fix is in place, Q.security verifies that it works. Monitoring of the organization’s cryptographic posture then continues as standards and threats change, an approach the company claims lets security teams reduce risk faster and at lower cost.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer, co-founder and chief executive of Q.security, who previously co-founded Unbound Security and led its research and development through its acquisition by Coinbase Global Inc., announced in 2021.

Peer’s co-founder, Nir Steinherz, was director of product at Coinbase and vice president of strategy and product at Unbound Security. He was also a senior vice president at Citigroup Inc.’s Security Innovation Center, where he led secure digital banking initiatives for more than 100 million customers. The pair are said to have led a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

The funding is intended to support Q.security as it brings its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partners.

Castle Island Ventures led the seed round, with New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund and Ground Up Ventures also participating.

Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures, said enterprises know they need to prepare for the day quantum computers can break current encryption. With harvest-now, decrypt-later data collection already under way, “the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” he added.

#5368. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5366. Mortgage headlines aren’t as big a concern as your cost per closing

The piece frames 2027 as a consolidation year, with equity strong but deal counts pressured by affordability. It urges teams to track cost per closing by source, stress-test a 20% volume drop, and shift toward sellers, sphere and longer follow-up.  AI Summary

If you run a real estate team, several weeks ago you probably saw and heard the chatter about potential rate hikes as high as 9% in 2027.

I understand why it spread. Freddie Mac had the 30-year fixed at 7.28% on Oct. 1, up from 6.01% in February and the Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. If everything moves the wrong way at once, 9% could sound possible.

The Real Estate Agent Facebook groups were bubbling about this in the comments. It is likely causing some anxiety for many agents.

It helps to look at what it would actually take. Cotality’s chief economist, Selma Hepp, raised 9% on CNBC as a worst case, not a forecast. HousingWire’s Logan Mohtashami laid out the math: the 10-year would have to push past 6%, and mortgage spreads would have to widen well beyond the roughly 2% they sit at today. That requires a hot economy, oil prices that stay high and a Fed that keeps hiking past what markets expect, all lasting well into next year. September’s jobs report showed 29,000 new jobs, which already works against the hot-economy part.

So I wouldn’t plan around 9%. I also wouldn’t plan around rates falling back to 6% anytime soon. The Fed’s own projections show no cuts in 2027, and the Mortgage Bankers Association expects rates to stay close to where they are.

A crash needs forced sellers, and we don’t have many. Homeowners with a mortgage carry an average loan-to-value of about 44%, and only around 2% are underwater, according to Cotality. That isn’t 2008.

What we do have is fewer deals. In early October, pending sales were about 10% less than the year before, and purchase applications were down 14%. Those applications turn into closings 30 to 90 days later, so a lot of teams have been looking at a softer first quarter. At today’s rate, the payment that covered a $400,000 loan in February covers about $357,000 now. Same buyer, same budget, about 11% less loan.

Prices mostly hold, and the deal count shrinks. I think of 2027 as a consolidation year rather than a crash year.

In August, I wrote here that cost-per-lead is the wrong number to run a team on, and that cost-per-closed deal is the one that tells you the truth. A slow year is when that stops being a philosophy and turns into a real potential problem.

Most of what a team spends to generate business is fixed. The ad campaign, vendor contracts, the ISA hours and the coaching all get billed whether deals close or not. When conversion falls, none of those invoices get smaller.

Say a team spends $6,000 a month on lead generation and closes 12 deals a quarter from it. That’s $1,500 per closing. Then buyer conversion slips, and the same spend produces nine closings. Now each closing costs $2,000. Nothing on the invoice changed, and every deal got a third more expensive.

That’s the exposure I’d worry about: a cost structure built for a 6.5% market, running in a 7.5% one.

The gap between a team that knows its number and one that doesn’t gets much wider when volume drops.

You can’t control the 10-year Treasury. These are the things you can control though:

Find your cost per closing by source. Add up everything you spend on each lead source, including ad spend, platform and referral fees, ISA time and software, and divide it by the closed transactions that source produced over the last 12 months. Use closings, not appointments or signed agreements. Most team leads I talk to have never broken this out by source, and the answer usually surprises them.

Stress-test it at a lower deal count. Run the same numbers assuming 20% fewer closings. Any source that ends up costing more per closing than your net is one to fix or cut now, while you still have room to choose.

Shift your mix toward sellers and your sphere. Buyers are the first to stall when rates jump. Sellers still have to move for new jobs, divorces, estates, and growing families, whatever the rate happens to be, and your past clients are sitting on real equity. If most of your pipeline is buyer leads, 2027 will hurt more than it should.

Lengthen your nurture instead of cutting it. The buyer who is priced out at 7.5% may be ready at 6.75%. If your follow-up ends at 90 days, someone else gets that deal if rates turn, and you end up paying for the same lead twice.

Give your agents training so they can handle these clients. Don’t promise rates will fall. Understand the concern first, then help the buyer evaluate actual numbers without treating a forecast as a fact.

2023 had the fewest existing-home sales since 1995. The teams I watched hold up through it weren’t the ones that guessed right about rates. They were the ones that knew what each closing cost them and kept moving money toward what was working.

There will be another very scary hot topic after this one, and another after that. The best hedge against all of them is the same: know your cost per closing, and build a pipeline that doesn’t depend on buyers feeling good about rates.

Robyn Thompson DeSantos is the founder and CEO of Ascension Group, a business solutions and management company for real estate team leaders and brokers.

#5365. Bootstrapped startup Levenza brings consumer-style personal agents to business workers

Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.

Levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it says are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees. The startup today announced the general availability of its enterprise-grade personal agents, together with its first acquisition in the shape of the AI research lab Fluid Inference.

In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups. The biggest name is probably Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, a “secure by design” personal assistant that quickly shot to the top of U.S. app charts following its launch in September. We’ve also seen OpenAI’s Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, which aim to proactively get work done on behalf of their users, as well as startups such as Instinct, which raised a colossal $1 billion in funding in September for its consumer-focused agents.

AI agents may still be somewhat divisive, but the early success of Muse, Dots and Instinct shows that there’s clearly a large market for automated assistants. Yet those tools are all targeted primarily at consumers rather than enterprise workers, which means there’s a massive gap in the market that’s waiting to be filled. Levenza wants to be the one that fills it, with its personal agents developed specifically to run inside sensitive corporate environments.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Haefa Mansour (pictured, left) told SiliconANGLE that the difference between Levenza’s agents and those of its competitors is that it takes time to work with individual companies to customize what they can and can’t do. She explained that workplace agents can only provide value if they’re able to connect to corporate systems securely and respect a company’s dynamics and security policies.

“People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside of work, and they’re expecting the same experience inside the office,” Mansour said. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, cha50sing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

Levenza’s personal agents are designed to live inside of the platforms where work gets done, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Slack. Within those environments, they act as proactive digital assistants for senior executives and other professionals.

Among other things, they can coordinate meetings across time zones, book hotel rooms, liaise with travel agencies, submit timesheets, triage overflowing email inboxes and send out replies and follow-ups when necessary. The more they do this work, the more they learn about the individual worker they’re serving, allowing them to become more useful over time, Mansour said.

By automating and coordinating routine work, Levenza’s agents can free workers from the “administrative drag” that affects every worker, slowing down productivity. “Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day and is interrupted every two minutes,” Mansour said. “On top of the inbox and the calendar come the travel, expenses and follow-ups that slip through the cracks – none of this is work that professionals were actually hired to do.”

Mansour, a former Bain & Co. alumni who holds a Ph.D. from the University of California, founded Levenza alongside former Databricks Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. engineer Austin Tackaberry (right) specifically to eliminate these distractions. The startup has made impressive traction, and despite not raising a dime in outside funding, its personal agents are already up and running at more than 300 enterprise customers, serving more than 10,000 professionals at those customers.

Early adopters such as Hg Capital and Oliver Wyman LLC report that their employees are saving up to three hours daily by offloading mundane admin to Levenza’s personal agents. They can also deal with any problems that occur during someone’s day. “For instance, if a manager’s customer workshop is running late and they’re likely to miss their flight, they don’t need to worry,” Mansour said. “Levenza will reach out to the travel management company to rebook according to their updated schedule.”

This means the manager in question will be able to focus on the workshop, safe in the knowledge that they’ll still be able to get to where they need to go after it does finish.

The acquisition of Fluid Inference is all about making Levenza’s agents more accessible. Mansour said the startup is an open-source research lab that’s focused on developing AI speech and ambient intelligence models.

By buying it, Levenza will be able to integrate natural voice interactions with its agents, so workers won’t have to tell them what needs to be done. Fluid Inference’s founder Brandon Weng is going to stick around as Levenza’s new head of engineering, adding much-needed talent to its team.

With Levenza’s agents now generally available, Mansour says the company will use its growing revenues to expand its third-party integrations and develop more capabilities for them. The company plans to launch automations for travel booking and expense management early next year, but that’s just the beginning.

“In the future, Levenza agents will operate with full autonomy in the enterprise, proactively deciding what work needs to be done,” she said. “They’ll coordinate with groups of other Levenza agents to collectively accomplish tasks.”

#5364. ABB helps scale industrial AI with world's first motor featuring built-in intelligence

ZURICH, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ABB today launched Intelleqtâ¢, the world's first low-voltage motor with intelligence integrated at the factory, designed to deliver real-time operational insights from its first rotation. Its open architecture enables customers across industries to connect motor data to their existing digital platforms while retaining full ownership of their data. By delivering equipment-level intelligence through a plug-and-play solution, Intelleqt helps companies build the data foundation needed to scale AI-driven operations.

Intelleqt arrives as industries increasingly seek to move artificial intelligence from pilot projects into core operations, with data quality and availability remaining among the main barriers to adoption. Industrial AI can deliver measurable value, but scaling its deployment remains challenging.

While 84 percent of manufacturers report benefits from artificial intelligence, only 20 percent of AI use cases have successfully scaled.1 At the same time, the equipment powering critical sectors such as data centers, water infrastructure and food production remains one of the largest untapped sources of operational intelligence.

More than 300 million motor-driven systems operate worldwide, accounting for 60 percent of industrial electricity demand2. Yet most are not connected to the digital technologies used to improve reliability, efficiency and performance. As electrification, automation and industrial AI accelerate, the $18 billion global IEC and NEMA low-voltage motor market is also positioned for further expansion.

"ABB's investment in research and development is always focused on solving real customer challenges," said Stefan Floeck, President of ABB's IEC Low Voltage Motors division. "The shift towards AI-driven operations is accelerating, yet most of the motors powering global industry do not generate data and remain invisible to the intelligence being built around them. ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is a world first that opens a new chapter in motor development, transforming motors from mechanical equipment into sources of real-time intelligence."

By turning motor data into actionable insights, ABB Intelleqt helps customers improve reliability, increase productivity and identify energy saving opportunities of 30 percent or more3. Early fault detection can reduce unplanned downtime by up to 50 percent4, helping industrial operators avoid failures costing up to $1.5 million per incident5. Factory-integrated sensing, edge computing and connectivity give customers access to these insights from day one.

ABB Intelleqt is the latest example of ABB's investment in artificial intelligence and digital technologies, bringing equipment-level intelligence to one of industry's most important and widely used assets while helping customers build the data foundation for the next generation of industrial AI.

Launched today at the SPS trade fair in Germany, ABB Intelleqtâ¢ is now entering a customer co-creation phase, working closely with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and end users to develop solutions tailored to their operational needs. A broader rollout is planned for 2027, initially focusing on markets in Europe, Japan, China and India.

ABB drives shared success with customers through innovation and customer-focused research and development. Drawing on more than 140 years of engineering expertise, ABB plans to invest 4.5 to 5.0 percent  of Group revenues in R&D to support the development of pioneering technologies such as ABB Intelleqt. In 2025, ABB invested $1.3 billion in R&D. The company has around 7,800 R&D employees across facilities in more than 30 countries on six continents, with approximately half focused on digital and software development. Since 2022, ABB's total R&D investment has increased by around 30 percent.

#5362. FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs

FHA’s 2026 Annual Report to Congress shows its HECM reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile part of the Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund. The HECM standalone capital ratio fell from 24.06% to 5.43% in one year, driven by slower home price growth, fewer loan payoffs and heavy assignment claim spending, though it stayed above the 2% statutory minimum.   AI Summary

The Federal Housing Administration’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress says the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year.

The report, released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund’s overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund’s statutory minimum requirement of 2%.

Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows.

The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund’s insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher.

The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers.

While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities (HMBS) market.

The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion.

Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026.

But even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand.

To fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors.

“I think that product diversity is great because we’re able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn’t handle,” Jesse Allen, president of 55+ lending at Rate, told HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo.

He said these may be “mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals,” but they can also be clients who don’t fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt.

“This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. ‘Hey, we’re paying off consumer debts. Let’s not count that toward the the qualification process.’ Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not,” Allen said.

FHA’s FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts.

The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios.

Home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives.

The report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities.

The stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums.

In September, Ginnie Mae President Joe Gormley told RMD that the Trump administration is “very comfortable” with the current mortgage insurance structure for FHA single-family loans and reverse mortgages. Gormley’s comments prompted pushback from NRMLA, which said it would continue to “dialogue with them around more risk-based pricing.”

An industry professional who was granted anonymity was more blunt in calling for lower premiums.

“The reality is this, if a client has to pay 2% to obtain the right to draw up to 30% of their home’s value, they will seek out other options,” the source said. “It should come as no surprise that HEIs and HEAs have been popping up everywhere. Even the gains on the proprietary side are the result of FHA’s inaction. Clients would rather accrue 10% interest annually to a lender than pay 2% upfront to a government insurer.”

The FHA report’s policy section does not identify any major new structural changes to the HECM program, but it does highlight several items of operational relevance.

This includes contract funding reallocation for assigned HECM property preservation expenses. FHA mentions a reallocation of contract funding tied to property preservation on assigned HECM collateral. While it’s a technical issue, it could affect vendors and servicers who manage preservation and conveyance on properties with HECM balances that are acquired by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

Fraud detection, data analytics and remediation were also mentioned. These areas are not limited to the HECM portfolio and apply across FHA single-family programs. Given the growing population of senior borrowers and the history of consumer protection scrutiny for reverse mortgages, these efforts may lead to tighter oversight of origination practices and borrower counseling outcomes in the HECM channel.

FHA also discussed ongoing system modernization efforts, including those tied to FHA Catalyst modules and uniform appraisal data initiatives. Over time, the report explained, better data capturing should improve the accuracy of HECM-backed property valuations — a key driver of assignment timing and loss estimates — and could result in more precise disclosures for HMBS investors.

The report also placed attention on the new permanent loss-mitigation waterfall for FHA forward mortgages that went into effect at the end of 2025. While that waterfall does not directly apply to HECMs, it signals a broader effort by the agency to standardize workout options and reduce cycles of repeated defaults. This approach could inform any future redesign of default resolution frameworks for reverse mortgages.

#5361. Hyperliquid Monero Crashes? Wagyu-Linked XMR1 Collapses, $13.2M Flows Into Ethereum

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

A Monero token crashed 99% on Friday after 5.2 million XMR1 tokens moved from a wallet tied to its creator, triggering a massive sell-off on Hyperliquid. The token, issued through crypto swap service Wagyu, plunged from around $494 to below $1 in 35 minutes. The wallet receiving the tokens sold enough to generate $13.22 million in USDC before converting the proceeds into 7,467 ETH.

Wagyu’s wallet security and the backing behind its wrapped Monero product are being questioned. And the sell-off also sent shockwaves through the Monero market, although native XMR remained a separate asset from the collapsing XMR1 market.

The incident began this morning when the account responsible for deploying XMR1 transferred tokens to a newly created wallet. Blockchain intelligence firm Bitquery identified three separate transfers between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. Two transactions moved 100,000 XMR1 each, followed by a much larger transfer of 5 million tokens.

The receiving wallet had been created that morning. It began selling shortly after receiving the tokens, overwhelming buyers on Hyperliquid’s order book. XMR1 had traded near $500 throughout the previous week. Its price then collapsed to about $1 within roughly 35 minutes, leaving holders with almost nothing.

Bitquery traced 363,804 tokens sold for $13.5 million. The remaining 4.83 million tokens stayed in the receiving wallet during its investigation. The sell-off also exposed how concentrated XMR1’s supply had been. Before the transfers, its deployer account still controlled 93% of the token’s supply.

Hyperliquid transfers require signatures from the account’s own key, rather than an ordinary trading API wallet. This means whoever authorized the transfers likely had access to the deployer’s main key. Whether someone stole that access or used it legitimately remains unknown.

The damage extended beyond traders watching XMR1 collapse on their screens. Bitquery matched the seller’s transactions against 388 accounts that purchased the dumped tokens. One buyer alone paid $3.56 million, while 27 large buyers accounted for 77% of the total proceeds.

The wallet did not leave the money sitting in USDC. It began moving funds through Hyperliquid’s bridge into Arbitrum shortly after selling.

XMR1 hack: 388 Hyperliquid buyers paid $13.50 million for a token that fell 99.8%https://t.co/k5ggHcH6Al

On Arbitrum, the wallet exchanged $13.22 million in USDC for 7,467 ETH through CoW Protocol. It then routed much of the Ethereum through Socket, Mayan, and Stargate. 6,810 ETH then arrived on Ethereum after those bridge transactions. Approximately 4,836 ETH landed in a newly created wallet that had not sent any funds onward.

The investigation also identified 7,348 ETH across three wallets during its tracking window. That left a substantial amount of the proceeds sitting outside the original trading account.

The incident has put Wagyu’s bridge infrastructure under scrutiny. XMR1 represents Monero on Hyperliquid and is issued through Wagyu’s bridging service. Users can move native XMR into the service and receive XMR1 for trading. They can also reverse the process to recover their Monero.

Native XMR did not suffer the same collapse. Monero continued trading around $470–$482, while XMR1 lost virtually all its market value.

Holders now face a difficult question: Can they still exchange their remaining XMR1 for native Monero?

The incident also comes weeks after Wagyu disclosed a separate data leak on October 28. Researchers identified exposed records potentially linking crypto deposits, Monero receiving addresses, and customer IP addresses.

Wagyu previously said customer funds remained unaffected by that incident. No established connection links the October leak to Friday’s wallet transfers.

The latest investigation also uncovered another potential concern. The same deployer account controls 99.97% of ZEC1, a separate token representing Zcash on Hyperliquid.

#5360. Innovaccer expands Gravity Voice AI agents with SpaceXSI’s Grok Voice model

Healthcare artificial intelligence company Innovaccer Inc. today announced that it has expanded its Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice, the speech-to-speech model from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXSI, formerly xAI.

The integration is aimed at the routine calls that make up much of a health system’s phone traffic, such as booking a visit, refilling a prescription or asking about a bill.

Grok Voice is a speech-to-speech model from SpaceXSI that is said to offer subsecond time to first audio, native tool use and the ability to reason while it speaks. According to Innovaccer, the model was trained on real phone audio with interruptions, corrections and background noise in it. More than 25 languages are supported. A business associate agreement is available for Grok Voice, which is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act-eligible.

Coming into the expansion, Innovaccer’s voice business has grown quickly. Patient voice interactions on the platform have gone from roughly 250,000 to more than five million in the six months since the agents went live. Customers using them are said to be booking significantly more appointments, with referral intakes tripled and documentation time per case down 90%.

“Healthcare Voice AI is moving from answering questions to doing work,” co-founder and Chief Executive Abhinav Shashank said. With Grok Voice, he said, the company is extending where its agents work across the healthcare journey.

Innovaccer’s Agents of Care on Gravity approach is designed so that software handles the bulk of administrative calls, such as scheduling and refills. A human stays in the loop on clinical conversations.

Existing customers will get Grok Voice first through upgrades, along with new customer deployments. Innovaccer plans to use it in scheduling, referrals, prior authorizations, refill requests, chronic care check-ins and annual wellness visit outreach, among other tasks.

The integration is set to extend beyond voice over time. Innovaccer says it will bring Grok models to its healthcare data through the Grok API, with plans for SpaceXSI’s Grok Build coding agent and Grok Bot AI agent as well. Healthcare-specific training and evaluation are to follow once the voice integration is live.

The integration comes about six weeks after SpaceXSI released Grok Voice 3.0, the latest version of the model. At the time, SpaceXSI said Starlink uses Grok Voice to answer about 20,000 customer calls a day, with roughly 70% resolved without a human. The SpaceXSI name was adopted earlier in October, following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI in February and a rename to SpaceXAI in July.

Innovaccer is a venture capital-backed company that has raised about $675 million to date, including a $275 million Series F round in January 2025. Notable customers include Orlando Health, Adventist HealthCare and Banner Health.

Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice capabilities are available now.

#5358. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”
