#5318. The Best Publicity Isn’t a Headline. Here’s What Built My Business Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I get a lot of LinkedIn requests, but I don’t connect for the sake of connecting. A thoughtful note and a 15-minute call have done more for my business than any press hit.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning shows and turned product launches like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and launched my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

If you’re connected to me on LinkedIn, we’ve talked. That’s on purpose. I get a lot of requests, but I don’t connect just to connect.

My filter is simple: a thoughtful note, or a profile that makes me curious. When someone clears that bar, I message them, introduce myself and suggest a 15-minute intro call by phone or Zoom. You can call me while you’re commuting, cooking dinner or taking a walk. I like to get to know the person first, then the business.

LinkedIn Premium is what makes this work for me. Seeing who’s viewed my profile tells me who’s already curious, and messaging lets me reach people with a personal note instead of a cold request. It’s what I’ve always done at conferences and events: walk across the room, say hello and ask how someone’s really doing.

A couple of years ago, I reached out to someone this way. We had two phone calls. No pitch, no deck, just getting to know each other.

After that second call, he referred me to two prospective clients. When I spoke with them, they told me something I’ll never forget: “If Michael trusts you, then we trust you.”

That sentence is the whole lesson. In PR, we talk about earned media versus paid media. Relationships work the same way. Trust that someone else earned with you and passed along is the most powerful credential you’ll ever have, and no ad can buy it.

A network you actually know pays off in another way: it’s the best search engine I have. When I need a partner or a service, I go to my network first. “Does anyone have a stellar digital growth performance agency?” gets me answers from people whose judgment I already trust, which beats a page of search results every time.

Being picky pays off here, too. Over the years, the people I know well have become my own personal advisory board.

The other half of building my own presence has been content. I publish a newsletter on LinkedIn called Spreading Sunshine. It’s personal by design. I share the latest in health and wellness, including my own protocols, along with business tips and a little joy. Readers tell me it feels like a note from a friend, which is exactly the point.

People now reach out because of what I post. The content does the introducing for me. By the time we get on that 15-minute call, they already know what I care about, and the conversation starts three steps ahead.

A personal profile and a company page do different jobs, and founders need both. SMACK! Media has its own page. When I launched Anything Brands, an all-natural skin remedy balm inspired by my own family, we set up a page for it, too.

My team uses the company pages for press hits, milestones and education. My personal page is where relationships happen; the company page is where credibility lives. When a retailer, a partner or a reporter looks us up, they find a consistent story in both places, and a founder they can actually reach.

Treat your network like your most important client. Be selective. Be generous. Show up as a human.

Ready to put that into practice? LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make those 15-minute conversations easier to start.

My favorite part is still the people: hearing about a founder’s big win, how someone got through a tough quarter, their kids, their dogs, how they juggle it all. If one of those calls leaves someone a little less burned out, that’s part of what fuels my positivity and boundless energy.

Some of my best relationships started with someone on the other end of the line, a little out of breath from a walk or with dinner sizzling in the background. Those calls rarely feel like business. After 30 years, I’ve learned the best publicity isn’t a headline. It’s someone who knows you saying your name in a room you’re not in. That’s exactly what Michael did for me. Treating myself like a client has been the best campaign I’ve ever run.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning shows and turned product launches like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and launched my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

#5317. As FEMA pushes recovery onto states, a Miami startup pitches an AI case manager for disaster survivors

When the Palisades fire tore through his Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, Jonathon Nostrant’s house was damaged but still standing. Many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed.

The fire was only the first ordeal. Next, Nostrant encountered a tangle of federal, state, and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules, and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers.

Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades. A year before the fire, State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned.

“Our insurance was fighting with us,” Nostrant said in an interview, describing his own claim.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant cofounded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules, and prepare applications. Survivors review everything before submission. The intended customers, though, are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner.

For now, it is a pitch. AidFinder hasn’t signed its first state customer, and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17. Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to listen. In 2008, as a student at the University of Southern California, he launched Moshi, a voice-activated alarm clock that responded to spoken commands and, in hindsight, foreshadowed Siri.

He later founded Ivee, an early AI-powered home assistant that let users control connected devices by voice. AidFinder applies the same idea to a far messier problem: turning a survivor’s account of what happened into the right applications for the right agencies.

The pitch arrives as Washington pushes more of the recovery burden onto states. FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton has told state emergency managers to prepare to handle more of the work themselves, and states have faced unusually long waits for federal disaster declarations.

Recounting Hamilton’s remarks at a National Emergency Management Association gathering, Nostrant described the federal message this way: “We want to empower the states, and we want to help empower the local counties and cities to be equipped, not just to respond to the disaster but help people recover.”

AidFinder’s answer is a branded front door. “We’re giving the state the ability to launch a landing page that’s powered by AidFinder,” Nostrant said, describing how residents would be matched with recovery programs.

Whatever tools states adopt, recovery paperwork starts with evidence. FEMA advises survivors to photograph or film damage inside and outside their homes before cleanup and to list damaged belongings, records that support both an insurance claim and a federal aid application.

AidFinder is built around the same principle. Its platform lets residents store identification, tax records, and photos of their homes in a secure digital vault before disaster strikes. The question now is whether a state will pay to offer it.

#5316. Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

“None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5315. AI agent provider Sierra closes $1.75B investment amid rapid revenue growth

Six months after its last funding round, artificial intelligence startup Sierra Technologies Inc. today announced that it has closed a $1.75 billion late-stage investment.

Greenoaks and Lightspeed led the Series F deal. They were joined by a group of returning backers that included Alphabet Inc.’s GV fund.

Sierra sells a set of cloud services that enables workers to create AI agents without writing code. The centerpiece of the suite is Ghostwriter, which can automatically generate agents based on user-provided prompts and files. A software team, for example, could upload a set of bug reports and request an agent that can automatically group them by problem type.

Ghostwriter checks the dataset that users upload for formatting errors before putting it to use. Once an agent is ready, the tool simulates user conversations to find potential bugs. Ghostwriter places particular emphasis on edge cases, unusual requests that can trip up an agent if they’re not addressed during development.

Sierra also offers a second development tool called Horizon. It can be used to create agents that automate time-consuming tasks. A marketing team could build an agent that monitors user interactions with a product page over several months, finds areas for improvement and automatically makes the necessary optimizations.

Sierra powers customers’ agents using more than a dozen large language models. Simple requests are sent to latency-optimized LLMs, while more complex queries are processed by pricier frontier models. Sierra says that it also uses several internally developed algorithms.

Customers can manage their AI projects using a third Sierra product called Agent Studio. According to the company, it includes over 40 connectors that enable agents to retrieve information from external systems. There’s also a tool for building custom connectors.

Agent Studio detects gaps in agents’ knowledge. Furthermore, it can automatically fix some of those gaps. The platform detects when a human support representative answers a customer inquiry that the help desk hasn’t encountered before and turns it into a knowledge base article. From there, agents can use the article to answer similar requests.

The studio also lends itself to certain other tasks. A collaboration feature enables multiple team members to review agent updates before they roll out to production. If a technical issue makes it past the review, developers can use a debugging tool to study what went wrong. The tool displays every single step of the workflow through which an agent processes prompts.

Rounding out Sierra’s product portfolio is an AI assistant called Explorer. It can proactively flag notable business events without a prompt and search through a company’s internal datasets. In some cases, it also generates business advice.

Sierra’s latest raise, its third in 14 months, comes a few weeks after its annualized revenue topped $400 million. The company disclosed at the time that it had added nearly half the sum over the preceding quarter. Its customer base now includes half the Fortune 50.

Sierra will reportedly use the new funding to enhance its product portfolio and hire more salespeople.

#5314. ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5313. A selloff, a POTUS, or a recession: What really made Nvidia bring Jensen Huang back as CEO?

The instant the news hit the wires Monday morning that Jensen Huang was back in the job as Nvidia CEO, shares of the AI chipmaker surged 29% in premarket trading. They went on to notch their best session in more than 20 years, while the broad-market S&P 500 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq jumped about 4.7% and 6.5% respectively.

What a change from last week, when the markets flashed red for two days and closed Friday in correction territory.

The news, at least for Monday, appears to have revived the AI trade and helped erase more than a week’s worth of losses for both the equities market and the tech behemoth.

Still, as investors celebrated and President Donald Trump took credit for Huang’s return, the big question looming over the stunning sequence of events revolved around cause and effect. Were the selloff and the Monday rally both reflections of Huang’s essential role in the global economy? Or was last week’s decline the result of broader, and still unresolved, instability in the markets that conveniently armed Huang’s supporters with a rationale to bring him back?

The sudden change of mind within Nvidia’s board—insisting the former CEO had no future at the company last week, and then saying exactly the opposite on Monday—added to the questions and sense of intrigue. What led the company to change its mind so abruptly, and why now?

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, wasn’t surprised that the selloff might have pushed the board’s hand. “There is a good reason to think that, with shareholders in play, they would think maybe, ‘We need Jensen back just because the market is telling us so much now,’” he said. Tigay pointed to Nvidia’s blowout earnings report last week without Huang at the helm, adding that although the firm beat expectations, the stock still couldn’t catch a break.

“The fundamentals of the stock were amazing, but the company is fundamentally different without Jensen. He is a visionary,” Tigay told Fortune. “He just has this longer-term view of where the technology is going and has been leading Nvidia correctly on that path for a long time. I think the stock market and shareholders wanted Nvidia with him and that vision.” (Equity Armor Investments, a wealth management firm, is an investor in Nvidia.)

Governance experts shared similar sentiments. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia is clearly an attempt to restore market confidence and prevent further losses after Friday ended in correction territory,” Nick Reese, a professor at New York University’s School of Professional Studies Center for Global Affairs, told Fortune.

That said, many of the long-standing causes of investor unease, particularly Nvidia’s role as the “central bank” financing a vast array of startups and potentially masking the true state of demand, have not gone away. If anything, Huang’s return could make the practice less likely to end (indeed, during Huang’s brief absence, Nvidia’s interim CEO had indicated a willingness to reassess some of the financing activities). And public backlash to building data centers, a key issue that helped Democrats sweep the recent U.S. midterm elections, is only likely to increase going forward—a significant headwind to the AI boom.

For Huang’s supporters, including a very vocal cohort of tech founders and billionaires, the stock market selloff in recent days was proof positive of Huang’s importance and a warning sign of larger economic danger.

“POTUS and JD’s intervention this weekend prevented a massive economic own goal this week for the US,” venture capital investor Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X on Monday. “They gave the Board what they needed to bring Jensen back.”

Trump trumpeted his role, telling CNBC on Monday that he spoke with Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly” and urged members to bring Huang back. “I convinced them,” Trump said. “I made the deal.”

“People say, ‘Is it a threat to have him?’ No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said of Huang. “I’m very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly.”

To be sure, Trump may have his own money in Nvidia. CNBC reported that investment accounts tied to the president have made 103 trades since he returned to the White House. Those transactions were worth a cumulative $27 million to $97.5 million. The White House says that Trump doesn’t control those trades, and that they are made by outside advisors.

Washington could have something to lose without Huang as well: America’s position in the AI race. “I think that even the biggest China hawks thought, ‘Gosh, if this has reduced [Nvidia’s] market capitalization, and U.S. companies might pull back on their investments in AI … does this pose a threat to America leading in AI?’” said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.

After all, there are several ways the U.S. could lose ground. Nvidia shed roughly $1 trillion in market value in the days after Huang resigned, and a long CEO search could have made companies think twice about funding the AI build-out that its chips power. Chinese customers might also move faster to domestic chips. And Washington would lose an executive who has spent years lobbying to sell American chips abroad.

Finally, there are economic concerns. Without Huang at the helm, Moorhead said, “this could take us into a recession.” AI investment has become one of the main engines of U.S. growth, adding roughly 1.3 percentage points to real GDP growth over the past three quarters, Reuters reported Monday, citing Apollo Global’s data. If Nvidia’s slump scared companies into pulling back, the economy would lose a substantial source of expansion.

But what’s next with Huang back on top? Analysts say the challenge is restoring confidence in Nvidia’s board. The board said in a statement that it acted after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government,” and an investigation regarding Huang as a possible target of foreign intelligence efforts isn’t finished yet.

“I think the board of Nvidia has some severely lacking corporate governance. This just kind of proves that,” Ryuta Makino, a research analyst at Gabelli Funds, told Fortune. Gabelli Funds is also an Nvidia investor.

Stacy Rasgon, a senior analyst at Bernstein Research, struck a similar note. “While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like … and brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions,” he said in a Monday note to clients. Still, the firm upgraded Nvidia stock to outperform from market perform.

Morgan Chittum is a reporter at Fortune covering finance.

#5312. Your Customers Just Got an AI Agent. Is Your Business Ready to Talk to Them?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Personal AI agents are now customers. Here’s how businesses can prepare.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

Someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

We used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

The simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

And they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

That kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a company has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this new reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

First, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the issue of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Resist the instinct to default to blocking. Throughout history, we’ve seen what happens to companies that try to close a door that’s going to be kicked down regardless. Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

Big players are picking sides right now, with Amazon blocking personal agents and Shopify building a lane. It’s tempting to treat their moves as a test case, something to monitor from the sidelines until the winds blow in one definitive direction.

That would be a mistake. Sure, the headlines may change in a week; in the case of these specific AI agents and the companies that created them, there may be developments that complicate their rapid surge in the short term. But the shift is happening, and CX organizations can’t be lulled into a reactive posture.

Nobody has built the perfect system for this yet. But the companies spending this period of uncertainty getting their infrastructure ready will be the ones with real footing when the dust settles. Everyone else will still be reading the news, wondering what to do next.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

Meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

#5311. Anthropic’s Claude Ship automates the final stage of the software development pipeline

Anthropic PBC isn’t satisfied with having Claude just write new software. With a new update today, Claude now can tell developers when the code it has generated is ready to ship into production environments.

The company announced the launch of Claude Ship, which is a new suite of artificial intelligence agents capable of automating code reviews, bug fixes and approvals. The last one is the most interesting of those capabilities, because code reviews and fixes are nothing new for AI. But Claude’s ability to automatically approve code changes based on the policies predetermined by an organization’s developer team is a novel development that has not been seen before.

Claude Ship is an effort by Anthropic to eliminate the new bottleneck that has emerged in the code review and approval process at companies that have already adopted AI code generation tools. At those organizations, fresh code is being whipped up in double-quick time, and there are also AI agents for checking that code and providing fixes if it’s not working as hoped. But until now, the final review and approval process has always been performed by humans. Claude Ship changes that.

The idea is that human developers can delegate final approval authority to Claude, so now all they really have to do is determine the quality and security standards of the code they’re asking AI to create.

“Most teams want a person to approve every change and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line,” Anthropic said in a blog post. “But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code and we wanted everything after the pull request to move that fast too.”

Anthropic said Claude Ship consists of three parts. The first is Code Review, which is a tool that has been generally available for some time already. The other two are PR Steward and Claude Approvals, and they’re both still in beta.

PR Steward is designed to handle issues such as failing continuous integration checks, merge conflicts and feedback from Code Review. After each push, it will leave comments on what changes were made and how to roll them back if necessary.

Once PR Steward is done, Claude Approvals takes over. It works by applying an approval policy that’s left as a file in the codebase’s repository. The approval process can incorporate various elements, including the findings in Code Review and the organization’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.

Anthropic is urging early adopters to be cautious. Because Claude Ship is still in beta, it recommends running Claude Approvals in observe-only mode first. It also advises teams to begin with just one repository first, and set monthly spending limits so they can maintain more control over everything.

#5309. TSMC gains $158 billion in value in one day as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO

Asian stocks rallied on Tuesday after the board of Nvidia—the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom—voted Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership crisis that had battered the region’s AI supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), which makes Nvidia’s chips, surged 9.9%, the daily limit, adding 5.2 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($158 billion) to its market value in a single day.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 3.9% as the market returned from a three-day weekend, while South Korea’s KOSPI surged 6.2% and Taiwan’s TAIEX climbed 9%.

Tuesday’s rally marks a rebound after a brutal stretch for the AI trade. The TAIEX fell by 17.5% last week, its worst such drop since 1991, pushing regulators to impose market stabilization measures, such as banning short selling, over the weekend.

Foxconn and Wistron, which assemble AI servers around Nvidia’s chips, rose almost 10%. SK Hynix, the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, climbed 6.7%, while Samsung Electronics rose 6.6%. In Japan, Kioxia, Toshiba’s former memory chip unit, surged 10.0%, and Advantest, which makes chip-testing equipment, jumped 12.5%.

“This looks like a powerful relief rally, amplified by short covering and the sharp selloff that preceded it,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank, says. “The initial rebound could extend over the next few trading sessions, particularly in semiconductor-heavy markets such as Taiwan and South Korea, where earnings visibility has improved following [Jensen] Huang’s return.”

Yet the relief from Huang’s return will likely peter out as broader concerns about the AI ecosystem persist. “I would expect markets to become more selective over the coming weeks, as investors shift their focus back from Nvidia’s leadership to AI spending, earnings delivery and the Fed’s policy outlook,” Chanana adds.

Not every Asian market is having a good day. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index fell by 0.6%. “The Hang Seng and mainland Chinese markets have struggled to find support,” says Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone, a currency and derivatives broker. “Without a meaningful rotation back into Chinese AI and technology stocks, sustained upside looks challenging.”

Huang’s return comes less than two weeks after his resignation. He stepped down on Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who some U.S. intelligence officials believed was working with Chinese espionage, according to the New York Times.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is at the center of allegations that Nvidia chips were diverted to China. The company has denied the allegations.

Last week, the Commerce Department expanded export controls on AI processors to Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and Brazil; it also closed a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia chips housed overseas.

On Monday, the department added seven companies to its Entity List, including Megaspeed. In a Federal Register notice, the department said the companies posed a “significant risk” and acted contrary to the “national security or foreign policy interests” of the U.S. The added companies include firms in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore, including several Megaspeed affiliates.

The same day, Nvidia’s board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company said in a statement.

#5308. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

#5307. He Retired at 50. At 70, He’s Working 7 Days a Week on His Biggest Idea Yet.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Peter Castleman could have spent retirement playing golf — instead, he built WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform.

If you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and says he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a big idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

This isn’t the first company you’ve started or been a big part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health issues, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I said, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

When a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always said, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How big is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a big budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

What do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone says, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.

#5306. Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B

Amazon.com Inc. today announced plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc. and acquire its core technology.

The company didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. That’s nearly twice the valuation Decart reportedly received after its most recent funding round in May.

In August, reports emerged that the company had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC. The artificial intelligence provider reportedly sought to buy Decart for $6 billion but walked away from the deal in September. Rumors that Amazon could swoop in emerged the following month.

Decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the company’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold.

The company hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart announced its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.”

Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion.

The company says that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language of the host chip. They also optimize the models along they way. For example, the compiler that Amazon Web Services offers for its AWS Trainium machine learning chip uses quantization to compress models into a more memory-efficient form.

It’s unclear whether Decart positions DOS as an alternative to the default compilers provided with AI accelerators. According to Amazon, Decart has “worked closely” with its engineers since 2025 to optimize the performance of workloads deployed on its Trainium chips. The newest commercially available iteration of the chip, Tranium3, provides 2.52 petaflops of performance when processing FP8 data.

Amazon stated that the acquisition will help “further optimize both its inference and custom silicon performance.” According to the company, the goal is to not only speed up customers’ models but also lower their cost.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”

The acquisition doesn’t include Decart’s portfolio of internally developed AI models. Its two newest algorithms, Lucy 2.5 and Oasis 3, are world models that generate virtual environments based on prompts. The former algorithm is optimized for low-latency content creation, while the latter is designed to generate training data for robots.

#5305. Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”

— Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.”

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform launched in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” said Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

— Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

In a post announcing the new role, Sanders said she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

— The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

— Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

— Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/19 to correct that Charlie Trillingham worked for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business, not the Foster School itself.

#5304. Why is gas suddenly cheaper? Five factors driving the drop to $3.64 a gallon

The average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that’s 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only hace to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices.

“The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “But, given how things have developed, it’s not really a shock.”

So, why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It’s a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn’t any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump’s actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:

Despite some ongoing conflict, the combination of U.S. naval escorts, complicated oil tanker transfers, and pipeline bypass routes have allowed the Middle East to return to nearly 90% of its pre-war oil exports, even though prices remain elevated from high tanker contracting and insurance costs. The rising levels of oil exports—despite depleted strategic oil reserves worldwide—have helped the global oil benchmark dip slightly below $90 per barrel as of Monday.

Prior to the elections, Trump openly said he was delaying any major ramp-up in attacks until after the midterms. That warning was keeping oil prices inflated as oil markets anticipated more disruptions to global oil flows in November. While risks remain and no peace deal seems on the near-term horizon, the lack of an escalation has helped prices fall. “The biggest thing now is this looming uncertainty over whether there will be something concrete and long-lasting,” De Haan told Fortune.

From a simple supply-and-demand standpoint, fuel prices typically peak in the summer during the busy driving season and bottom out in the winter when more people are bundled up at home. Although there are brief travel spikes for Thanksgiving and Christmas, driving is typically muted near the end and beginning of each calendar year. Likewise, fuel is cheaper to manufacture during the colder months. Summer-grade gasoline is more expensive because of extra additives required to keep fuel components from evaporating in the heat. Winter-grade fuel is cheaper and less complex.

Globally, nearly 10% of refineries remain offline, largely in the Middle East and Russia because of wars. But, in the U.S., there also were supply disruptions at ExxonMobil’s Joliet and Phillips 66’s Wood River refineries in Illinois. Those temporary outages from weather issues and mechanical failures caused additional price spikes throughout the Midwest. “The refining issues were boosting prices ahead of the election,” De Haan said. “As these issues have been getting resolved, they’ve been pushing prices down, coupled with the seasonality, coupled with oil markets.” Outside of the Middle East and Russia, China also had mothballed some refineries during the Iran war. As China has depleted more of its own reserves, the country has of late ramped up its output, including its fuel exports, adding to global supplies.

Refining complexes aren’t built to operate like light switches for diesel or other petroleum products. When refineries are pushed to run at their maximum utilization levels for diesel, that also means increasing their volumes of gasoline. With diesel demand surging in the fall, the U.S refining industry is on overdrive and raking in record profits, often delaying planned maintenance work until next year. “Refineries are operating at their highest November rate since 1998,” De Haan said. “This may be the highest utilization year for refineries ever. It’s going to be really close.”

Fuel prices remain elevated, but there’s no hiding how far they’ve fallen. As such, nearly as many Americans as last year plan to travel for Thanksgiving. AAA projects 72.9 million people will travel on the road this Thanksgiving, only a slight drop from 73.1 million last year.

GasBuddy’s survey data showed that almost two-thirds of Americans plan to hit the road this week. Close to 20% of travelers said they will cut back on other holiday spending to cover the extra fuel costs.

If there are no more major energy disruptions in the Middle East, De Haan said, the national average for gasoline could bottom out as low as $3.35 per gallon over the next few weeks.

Jordan Blum is the Energy editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of a growing global energy sector for oil and gas, transition businesses, renewables, and critical minerals.

#5303. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI Predicts the Flippening: How Does ADA Flip XRP?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Could 2027 finally be the year Cardano (ADA) overtakes Ripple (XRP) in the cryptocurrency rankings? Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that, despite XRP’s established position among the industry’s largest digital assets, network upgrades, renewed institutional interest, and a shift in investor sentiment could make it more likely than it first appears.

Both cryptocurrencies have spent years competing for attention, albeit with very different propositions. XRP has built its reputation around cross-border payments and financial infrastructure, while Cardano has focused on research-driven development, decentralized applications, and a carefully structured ecosystem.

However, market leadership can change quickly during a cryptocurrency bull market. If Cardano delivers on its ambitious development roadmap while XRP struggles to maintain its momentum, the gap between the two could narrow considerably.

And while flipping XRP would require an extraordinary rally, ADA could climb to a valuation few investors currently anticipate.

One of Cardano’s biggest opportunities heading into 2027 is its ongoing push to improve network scalability.

The planned Ouroboros Leios upgrade is particularly important. Designed to increase transaction throughput without compromising Cardano’s decentralized architecture, Leios could address a longstanding criticism: its ability to compete with higher-throughput blockchain ecosystems.

Cardano’s Dijkstra development cycle also introduces further improvements, with Peras activation targeted for the second quarter of 2027. Peras is designed to improve transaction settlement speed by reducing the time needed to achieve stronger confirmation confidence.

Meanwhile, developments around programmable tokens, decentralized finance, and real-world asset tokenization could help Cardano attract applications that generate genuine demand for ADA.

These upgrades won’t automatically translate into higher token prices, but successful implementation could give investors a compelling reason to reconsider Cardano’s long-term valuation.

XRP has several advantages that Cardano cannot easily replicate. Ripple has spent years building relationships across the financial sector, while the XRP Ledger continues to expand into institutional decentralized finance, stablecoins, and tokenized real-world assets.

The network processed an average of approximately 2.48 million daily transactions during the first quarter of 2026, while its real-world asset market capitalization reached $2.25Bn. These are meaningful indicators of ecosystem activity.

However, XRP’s enormous market capitalization also creates a challenge for investors seeking outsized returns. With a much larger valuation than ADA, XRP needs substantially more capital inflows to achieve the same percentage gains.

Recent market comparisons have placed XRP’s valuation at roughly ten times Cardano’s, highlighting the scale of the challenge. If capital rotates toward smaller, established layer-1 networks during the next bull market, ADA could benefit disproportionately.

ADA previously reached an all-time high around $3.10 during the 2021 bull market, demonstrating that the cryptocurrency can attract substantial speculative demand when market conditions are favorable.

A sustained recovery towards its previous peak would be an important psychological milestone. However, a genuine breakout beyond that region would potentially open the door to a much larger valuation.

For XRP, the challenge is maintaining its market leadership while competing with an expanding range of payment-focused blockchain networks. Its established institutional presence provides a strong foundation, but continued adoption growth will be necessary to justify a substantially higher valuation.

The key technical signal to watch for ADA is a sustained sequence of higher highs and higher lows on the weekly and monthly charts, accompanied by improving relative strength against XRP.

A decisive break above previous cycle resistance, followed by a successful retest, could signal that a longer-term trend reversal is underway.

Explore: The Best Token Presales Right Now

Consider an optimistic scenario in which the broader cryptocurrency market enters another substantial bull phase during 2027.

Cardano successfully implements its major upgrades, DeFi activity expands, institutional interest improves, and investors begin viewing ADA as an undervalued alternative to larger blockchain assets.

Under these circumstances, a move towards $1.50–$2.50 becomes an interesting longer-term price scenario, with the upper end representing a substantial recovery towards its previous all-time high.

At $2.50, Cardano’s market capitalization would approach $95 billion, assuming a circulating supply of approximately 38 billion ADA. That would represent a significant increase from its current valuation.

However, overtaking XRP would depend on more than Cardano’s own performance. XRP’s valuation would also need to be considered, meaning ADA could reach $2.50 without necessarily overtaking its rival.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that Cardano has a genuine opportunity to flip XRP in 2027, with ADA potentially reaching $2.50.

Although XRP remains the more established cryptocurrency, Meta AI believes Cardano offers the more interesting upside opportunity if its development roadmap translates into meaningful ecosystem growth.

The deciding factor will be execution. If Leios, Peras, and Cardano’s broader adoption initiatives deliver, 2027 could be the year ADA finally challenges XRP’s dominance.

#5302. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”
