#5301. I Stayed On a Private Island in Fiji. It Pulls Off a Top Travel Trend With a Luxury Twist—Here’s What Any Hospitality Business Can Learn.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Kokomo Private Island offers a bespoke experience guests will dream about long after they return home.

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

Today, the property features 21 beachfront villas and five hilltop residences, each with a private pool; three principal dining venues, with more than 80% of herbs and greens sourced from the island’s 5.5-acre organic farm; the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with its dedicated fitness center; and no shortage of adventure and cultural activities available to its guests.

My husband and I had a chance to experience the tropical island paradise for ourselves in September. Throughout our stay, we were struck by Kokomo’s sheer natural beauty and how much the luxury hospitality experience was rooted in a genuine sense of place.

Increasingly, hotels and resorts highlighting local character rise to the top of travelers’ wishlists. Nearly three-quarters of luxury travelers won’t pay for accommodations that feel generic, per a report from Preferred Hotels & Resorts, and 77% of travelers prioritize authentic experiences representative of local culture, according to research from Booking.com.

Kokomo serves as a lesson in hospitality excellence — what it takes to succeed in a travel landscape increasingly defined by a desire for authenticity and local character. Here’s how every business can do the same.

After a long day (or more) of travel, first impressions are key. Guests want to feel at ease and an immediate sense of place. But, sometimes, that’s the straightforward part. Sustaining that genuine warm welcome throughout the stay also matters.

Staff members at Kokomo give it its personality and make guests feel at home, often forming relationships that bring people back year after year, Walker says.

Additionally, Kokomo has developed a close relationship with the local community, where some staff members are from: supporting local employment, working with neighboring villages, and contributing to education, healthcare and community initiatives.

“Authenticity comes from allowing those relationships and traditions to exist naturally, rather than trying to manufacture an experience for guests,” Walker says. “When someone shares a story about their village, introduces a guest to a local custom or folklore or even simply welcomes them with genuine Fijian hospitality, that’s what stays with people.”

Our arrival and journey to Kokomo was seamless from the first “bula” (Fijian for “hello” and a wish for life and good health). After a 45-minute seaplane ride, we touched down on the crystalline blue waters in front of Kokomo. We were given a salusalu, a traditional garland worn around the neck, and coconut water, and listened to a group of staff members sing traditional Fijian welcome songs.

That warmth and hospitality extended throughout our time at Kokomo, across the interactions we had with staff and when we visited the nearby Dravuni Village, which is home to a small indigenous Fijian community. We heard traditional songs, learned about their hand-woven crafts, participated in a kava ceremony and toured the village with a staff member who’d grown up there.

The business lesson is this: Lean into what makes a destination special, and the cultural touchstones that define it, for an authentic welcome that extends from the first moment to the last.

Of course, as much as people want to soak up all a destination has to offer, they’ll spend a good portion of their vacation in their accommodations. Ideally, those accommodations capture the destination’s unique characteristics while prioritizing comfort.

“For me, true luxury isn’t about formality,” Walker says. “It’s about comfort, freedom, being able to enjoy yourself without feeling constrained by the usual expectations of a hotel. Children should be able to run around, explore and have adventures, while their parents and grandparents can relax and enjoy the island in their own way.”

Our one-bedroom beachfront villa, just steps from the ocean, felt sprung from the tropical landscape itself. The high ceilings, neutral stone and wood, and ample windows, the better to display the expansive patio with its private pool and the dazzling ocean view, created an indoor-outdoor flow with understated natural elegance.

When it comes to architecture, interior design, or landscape, embracing what sets the place surrounding it apart from any other, rather than competing with it, helps establish that seamless, one-of-kind experience guests won’t forget.

Whether a guest is a serious gourmet or not, meals will stand out as part of the experience (a three-times-a-day touchpoint). For remote resorts where guests rely solely on the dining on-site, it’s even more critical to deliver elevated, locally-defined experiences.

Early on, the Walkers realized they had access to the best ingredients on their doorstep — fresh seafood and the climate and space to grow much of the island’s own produce — and built their culinary philosophy around that, Walker says.

“A fish caught locally that morning, vegetables picked from the garden, herbs cut just before they’re used,” she explains. “You can’t get much fresher than that. Building and operating a resort in such a remote location comes with enormous logistical challenges, so growing more of our own food and reducing our reliance on imported produce makes sense on many levels.”

We had a chance to go on a tour with Kokomo’s executive chef Marty Kindleysides. He gave us an inside look at the island’s farm and hydroponic gardens, which help shape the menus across its restaurants: the Beach Shack on Kokomo’s western beach; Walker D’Plank, featuring Asian-influenced cuisine, near the arrival jetty; and the poolside Kokocabana, highlighting Italian-inspired dishes.

From the beautiful lunch Kindleysides prepared for us with farm-fresh ingredients like squash and kale, to all of the meals we enjoyed at the other dining venues, including a showstopping dinner by Chef Caroline during a curry-themed night at Walker D’Plank, the food was flavorful, intentional and reinforced a singular dining experience.

Guests should never feel like the food where they’re staying is an afterthought; it’s another opportunity — and a very memorable one — to showcase innovation and what makes a setting unique.

At a remote tropical resort like Kokomo, guests have the luxury of a picture-perfect natural setting offering once-in-a-lifetime activities. But striking the balance between making the most of the environment and protecting it is also critical.

Lang was an avid diver for most of his life and immediately recognized the wonder of the Great Astrolabe Reef. The Walkers saw it as their responsibility to look after it, so they set out to help guests experience and understand it.

“There’s something quite powerful about a child helping to plant coral, or a family learning about the individual manta rays that return to our waterways each season,” Walker says. “Suddenly conservation becomes personal. You’re no longer looking at a beautiful reef, rather, you’re beginning to understand how it works and why protecting it matters.”

We had the opportunity to meet with a marine biologist to learn about the manta rays and conservation efforts. Kokomo has partnered with Manta Project Fiji to research and protect Fiji’s reef manta rays since 2017. More than 500 manta ray sightings were recorded during the most recent monitoring period. We even went to look for them by boat, but unfortunately with it being the tail end of the season, didn’t spot any.

Additionally, the marine biologist led us on a guided coral restoration tour, where we snorkeled over some of the current projects underway. More than 2,000 corals have been transplanted as part of Kokomo’s coral restoration. The island also has six active coral nurseries, which can support more than 10,000 corals per season.

Bringing guests into the very projects that protect the place they’re staying gives them destination-driven, extraordinary experiences while safeguarding them for future generations.

Relaxation means different things to different people, but centralizing spa and wellness options in one place, and melding personalized comfort with distinct ambiance, gives everyone the option to design an ideal routine to reset.

The Walkers wanted to build on the feeling guests have upon arrival — everyday life demands removed by the grandeur of nature — and developed the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with that in mind.

We enjoyed Kokomo’s signature “Pacific Mastery Massage,” which incorporates centuries-old methods from traditional Fijian Bobo, combining variable pressure and rhythmic movement with the preferred oil blend. Before and after the service, we sipped iced hibiscus tea (the flower is often seen in Fijian landscaping) in the garden setting.

Guests will remember how a vacation makes them feel, so making sure they have the option to truly unwind, whatever that looks like for them, is key. Infusing it with a local twist means they won’t forget exactly where they experienced it.

At the end of the stay, as we departed on the one-hour helicopter ride back to the hangar, spotting our villa on the lush island encircled by a shock of turquoise, we came away already nostalgic for the trip, and with a deeper appreciation for Fiji’s natural beauty and vibrant culture.

We would love to return some day (maybe to snorkel with the mantas) — and that’s exactly what the Walkers intended.

“More than anything, I hope guests leave Kokomo feeling they’ve been part of something special,” Walker says. “That they’ve spent quality time with the people they love, experienced the generosity of our Fijian team and discovered a part of the world they’ll always remember. If they leave feeling as though Kokomo is their island home, then we’ve achieved what we set out to do.”

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

#5300. Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie

The 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for the sport, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

American entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the WNBA—now an $850 million franchise— underlines the potential, and many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport.

U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.

Speaking at the WSL’s New Playbook ­ summit earlier this year, one investor argued that European women’s football represented the “best opportunity in sport,” on a risk-adjusted basis.

“I think of my career as if I’m still an athlete. I practice for every board meeting in the same way that I used to train for a game. Your practice should be so hard, the game is easy.”

“The enterprise value of these clubs is 100% going up,” Doucet, a former investment banker at Citi, says. “The question is, do you have owners that want to participate in this asset class of women’s football? There are different tradeoffs versus men’s football and different risk factors because we’re in a different stage of development.”

Doucet’s challenge is turning rising global interest in the women’s game into regular paying customers. There was a surge in interest following the England Lionesses’ UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 victory: Average attendance at WSL matches tripled to 5,616 the following season. But last year, median attendance was 3,236—and it remains heavily concentrated in a few clubs.

“This isn’t a manufacturing challenge. This is a marketing and revenue challenge,” Doucet says. The league invested in a rebrand of both the WSL and WSL2 ahead of the newly expanded league this season, and clubs are also investing more. In April, WSL team Brighton announced plans to build Europe’s first purpose- built women’s football stadium at an estimated cost of more than £75 million ($99 million).

“You have to invest in building the foundations that will generate long- term returns, but they might take time until you actually see the results,” Doucet says. “That’s the constant tradeoff.”

The underlying economics also remain fragile. Despite the high revenues, only four of the 14 clubs in the WSL recorded a profit (two clubs did not publish detailed financial data). The league itself, which is co-owned by the participating clubs, posted an operating loss of £8.2 million ($10.8 million) for the year ending July 2025.

Doucet attributes much of the loss to one-off costs associated with becoming an independent business, including establishing its own HR, finance, legal, and regulatory teams. The WSL and WSL2 formally split from the Football Association (FA) in 2024, shortly after Doucet joined the organization. She says the league is now profitable, although declined to share the financial details.

“We’re in a transition phase, which is probably a little bit messy. The challenge is going from big structural moments, like a World Cup, to building a weekly fan habit around women’s professional football,” Doucet says.

The majority of the league’s revenues so far have come from broadcast rights and commercial partnerships. The league generated £8.7 million ($11.5 million) from Sky and the BBC in 2025, and the league counts Doucet’s former employer Nike, in addition to Airbnb, Apple, and ­ Barclays, among its growing list of sponsors.

The opportunities for commercial sponsors are different from those in the men’s sport, Doucet says. “We have a different audience that really values companies that are investing in women’s football,” she says. “They’re very brand loyal, and they show much deeper engagement.”

Doucet’s current priority is improving the spectacle on the pitch. “The fans want to watch the best players, and they want to watch a competition that’s exciting and has jeopardy,” she says. Good progress has been made in this area, too. The London City Lionesses signed three-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas from Barcelona this summer, and the WSL had the highest representation of players at last year’s Women’s Euro tournament of any league.

Ensuring the WSL’s longevity is a responsibility Doucet is acutely aware of. “This isn’t a five-year business,” she says. “This is a generational asset.” She remains optimistic about what lies ahead. Doucet adds: “We’re in an early stage, so the potential is almost completely untapped—you don’t know how big it could be.”

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune with the headline “Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie.”

Sam Forsdick is editor – features and Fortune 500 C-Suite Europe at Fortune, where he oversees the European edition of Fortune magazine and edits the Europe section of the website. An experienced business journalist and editor, he has covered leadership, management, and workplace issues throughout his career. Previously, he has worked as managing editor of People Management, HR editor at Raconteur, digital editor of I – Global Intelligence for Digital Leaders, and features writer for Director magazine.

#5299. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5298. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5297. Engineer, saleswoman, Elon Musk whisperer: Meet Gwynne Shotwell, the billionaire who really runs SpaceX

The quiet billionaire who turns Elon Musk’s wildest ideas into revenue is facing her toughest test yet.

In 2002 Gwynne Shotwell had a lunch that would change her life—and the trajectory of the business world as we know it. Then 38, she had been working for a decade at a rocket startup, frustrated at the pace of innovation on the ground. “It wasn’t a vibrant industry, and we hadn’t gotten back to the moon [in 30 years],” she said on a podcast in 2022. “The systems were designed to eliminate risk, so they took forever and cost too much.” A former colleague had just departed for another rocket startup, and she met him to celebrate at a favorite Austrian restaurant in the coastal L.A. suburb of El Segundo. Afterward, her friend suggested Shotwell stop by his new company to meet the owner.

The owner, of course, was Elon Musk. Fresh off making a fortune at PayPal, Musk laid out his vision to the curious Shotwell: make rockets a lot more cheaply than NASA; sell launches to commercial satellite companies at super-bargain prices; slash prices even more by making the rockets reusable. Shotwell blurted out that he needed a “business developer,” effectively a sales leader who could win the pre-product contracts needed to fund the vision. Musk called her with an offer, and within days, Shotwell came aboard SpaceX. “I knew that working for Elon would be my last job in aerospace,” she has often said.

The investors and funds that have bought shares in SpaceX since its debut as, pre-Anthropic, the biggest IPO of all time are placing a huge bet on the visionary genius of Elon Musk. Though they may not realize it, those investors are also betting on the far lesser-known figure who’s spent two decades at Musk’s side turning his seemingly crazy dreams into big-money ventures. Now 63, Shotwell was employee No. 7 at SpaceX, and the IPO made her extremely wealthy: her 12.6 million shares were worth some $2 billion after the company went public. While Musk is SpaceX’s CEO, chairman, and chief technology officer (and controls around 40% of the shares), Shotwell’s the operator. As she put it in a recent interview, “He focuses on the future…on strategy and deep dives on the technical [side]. I focus on things that are helpful to customers today to earn money.” Shotwell doesn’t post on social media or seek publicity. She toils behind the scenes, mining Musk’s portfolio of futuristic ideas for the ones she can craft into cash-generating products.

Shotwell has achieved a spectacular record of tackling never-before-seen technological hurdles. She oversaw development of the Falcon 9, the world’s first orbital-class reusable commercial rocket, and helped make SpaceX the first private company to carry astronauts into orbit. Her cost breakthroughs enabled the Starlink galaxy of over 11,000 satellites, now SpaceX’s prime revenue and profit provider. Douglas Loverro, a former top official in the Air Force space program who’s worked extensively with Shotwell, told Fortune that for decades he’s believed that the only thing that makes money in space is communications and connectivity. “Elon and Gwynne saw it,” he observes. “Gwynne made it happen.”

But Shotwell’s job just got exponentially more difficult. Musk has rebranded SpaceX as an AI company, taken it public, and forecast a $1 trillion revenue run rate by 2030, a feat he plans to achieve largely by putting data centers in orbit. To get there, SpaceX more than tripled its capex to $48.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, and in August Shotwell unveiled a $100 billion Louisiana launch site to send them up. Skeptics, including some who won’t bet against Musk, doubt the economics can ever work. The numbers, observes Aswath Damodaran, a professor at NYU’s Stern School of Business, are “mind-blowingly large.” His biggest fear for SpaceX’s future is that “it overspends on orbital AI.”

The biggest thing working in Shotwell’s favor is that she has mastered a challenge that has defeated many others: managing Musk himself. As Walter Isaacson states in his definitive biography Elon Musk, the boss “doesn’t naturally partner with people. Collegiality is not part of his skill set. He inspires, frightens, bullies, and does not like to share power.” At Tesla, for example, Musk named one president who served just over two years, and never replaced him. Somehow, Shotwell’s rare combination of an engineering mindset, a knack for smoothly wooing customers, not to mention her money-making instincts, has fully captured Musk’s confidence.

People who’ve observed the pair in action credit Shotwell as the adult in the next cubicle. “I’ve worked with both Elon and Gwynne, and I’ve got to tell you, working with Gwynne is a lot more pleasant,” says one former client. As Isaacson told Fortune, “Gwynne’s indispensable to SpaceX, a perfect mind partner for Elon. She knows how to accomplish his goals while occasionally altering his trajectories and being engineering-honest with him, which is the way he likes to operate. She combines an engineering mind with a fingertip feel for how to deal with people.”

It’s a kind of odd-couple collaboration that works. Tom Mueller, SpaceX’s first employee and developer of the Merlin engine that powers the Falcon rockets, said in an email to Fortune that Shotwell brought a “unique skillset to the table that complements all the talent Elon was assembling.” In other interviews Mueller, who retired from SpaceX in 2020, put it even more simply: “I built the rockets, but Gwynne built the company.”

For 24 years Musk has supplied the vision, and Shotwell’s genius has been finding the money. Now she has to monetize the most expensive idea he’s ever had. The question is, Can she? Can anyone?

In her own way, Shotwell’s just as much a Big Personality as Elon Musk. Regularly attired in dark blazers, skinny jeans and super-high heels, sporting a flowing blond coif and typically, a crescent of pearls, she’s a born raconteur who describes herself as “a people engineer.” Today she and her husband, Robert Shotwell, a NASA engineer, are repurposing their ranch on the San Gabriel River in Texas as a vineyard. From the spread, Gwynne drives to work in a bright red Tesla Model S, a Starlink mini-dish strapped to the ski rack so she doesn’t drop the call when Elon phones.

For this story, SpaceX declined to make Shotwell available for interviews. She’s talked extensively to the mainstream or business media only a few times, though over the past 20 years she has spoken in depth to industry groups and at universities, including her alma mater Northwestern. Where not otherwise attributed, Fortune’s account of her background and career draws on those public statements and on Isaacson’s Elon Musk.

Gwynne Rowley grew up in the Chicago suburb of Libertyville, the middle daughter of an artist mom and a father who taught neurosurgery at Northwestern medical school. She relished fixing bicycles, but her career-sparking revelation came when her mother dragged the 15-year-old to a conference for the Society of Women Engineers. “I didn’t want to be there, I was a grumpy teenager,” Shotwell recalls. “I was interested in cheerleading and clothes. I thought of engineers as nerds and outcasts.”

But one mechanical engineer’s super-style black suit and elegant footwear knocked Gwynne out. “I went up and congratulated her on her suit,” says Shotwell. Suddenly, she decided engineers could be “cool.” But Shotwell doesn’t discount her glamorous high school avocation as training for the business world. “Cheerleaders make great salespeople,” she observes.

In 1986, Shotwell was one of three women in her class of 36 who graduated from Northwestern’s McCormick School of Engineering. Two years later, she joined Aerospace Corp., a nonprofit that advises government and commercial space programs, where she wrote papers modeling how heated and cooled satellite components work in tandem—a challenge that’s paramount for orbital data centers. But her real passion was designing and building spacecraft. So after 10 years, she joined Microcosm Inc., which won military and NASA contracts to architect rockets aimed at radically reducing the cost of sending satellites into space.

Then came the fateful lunch and meeting with Elon.

Shotwell’s mission: Selling contracts to military and corporate clients to fund development of the lowest-cost rocket ever produced. “If you don’t have a rocket to sell, what’s really important is selling the team,” recalls Shotwell. “Selling the technical savvy of your CEO and making sure you can address any technical issue right away.” Shotwell worked out of a cubicle next to Musk’s, and would even vacuum the conference room prior to client meetings. As Mueller told Fortune, “We were writing our own playbook across all aspects of the business, and she jumped in and became a contributor from day one.”

Indeed, Shotwell won clients for the maiden SpaceX launches from an atoll in the South Pacific, aboard its new Falcon 1 rocket, including NASA and the DOD. On the first three flights, the rockets either failed or exploded. Musk believed SpaceX had sufficient cash for two more attempts; Shotwell told Musk that he was being a Pollyanna, and that if the next one flopped, SpaceX would flame out, too. On the fourth liftoff day in September of 2008, Shotwell was in a hotel in Glasgow apologizing to customers who’d lost payloads on the earlier launches when, well past midnight, she watched the livestream of the Falcon 1 reaching orbit and carrying a dummy payload nicknamed RatSat that substituted for a satellite the Malaysian government pulled due to nervousness over the three failed flights. She relishes telling how she ran down the hotel corridor in her “jammies” yelling joyously, and commandeered the bar for a night of champagne and revelry.

“I built the rockets, but Gwynne built the company. We were writing our own playbook.“

That first successful launch landed SpaceX a $1.6 billion contract from NASA to deliver cargo to the International Space Station. The deal also inspired Musk to offer her the position of president at the close of 2008. She relates that at first, she “thought it was weird to be boss” and “my first reaction was ‘no.’” But after “a nanosecond of stupidity,” she said yes to Musk. Since then, SpaceX has made 36 cargo and 14 crewed launches to the ISS for NASA, long its biggest customer. In 2010, SpaceX introduced the Falcon 1’s successor, the 21-story-tall Falcon 9 that’s still its workhorse.

Shotwell’s a whiz at deploying templates to drive down costs. Instead of paying what she claims would have been $1 billion to develop an all-new engine for the Falcon 9, SpaceX packed nine of the Falcon 1’s Merlins into the booster; Starship, which will head its future fleets, carries a total of 39 Raptor engines developed in-house. Other solutions look improvised: Isaacson relates that, faced with an estimated cost of more than $3 million for Falcon 9’s payload-bay cooling system, SpaceX instead bought and modified commercial air-conditioning units priced at a few thousand each.

Shotwell also brings an intangible asset that’s essential to SpaceX’s rise: superb diplomatic skills. Loverro has marveled for two decades at how she maintains lucrative relationships after tough client encounters that could have closed the door. “Back in 2007, we were relying on America’s only rocket company that was charging ridiculous prices,” he told Fortune. Loverro negotiated with Shotwell for a year to launch a battlefield imaging satellite on the Falcon 1, and SpaceX won the bid. “Just when I was about to tell her she’d won, Gwynne calls to tell me they were shutting down Falcon 1 production.”

Loverro took plenty of flak from the Air Force brass, but remained convinced that Shotwell could deliver. A couple of years later, Congress committed $50 million for an experimental satellite launch that the Air Force feared would cost more. “I asked Gwynne, ‘Are you able to do it for $50 million?’ and she said yes, for that fixed price. Fixed prices were their specialty.”

The successful launch happened in 2015. “SpaceX was four years late, but they’re always late,” notes Loverro. Even after Musk famously sued the U.S. Air Force for awarding contracts to a rival sans competitive bids, government business kept flowing to SpaceX, and Loverro awards much of the credit to Shotwell. “Imagine your company is suing the government, but someone has to do business with the government anyway! That was Gwynne.”

Shotwell can even do something that many have deemed impossible: Get Musk to change his mind. Isaacson relates that in 2019, Musk impulsively decided to shutter the Falcon Heavy. Shotwell sped to his cubicle, reminded Musk that SpaceX needed its then-biggest vehicle to fulfill a major military contract, and got him to nix the cancellation. According to the biography, she also denounced Musk’s promise to award the Pentagon free use of SpaceX internet service to his face as “ridiculous,” and made sure Starlink got paid. In interviews, she proudly describes herself as blunt and “mouthy,” and according to Isaacson, skewers longtime lieutenants who won’t stand up to Musk, calling them “chickens.”

Still, Shotwell’s in many ways just as tough a boss as Musk. She admits that Musk “does create uncomfortable situations in the office,” and though her style’s far more agreeable, Shotwell is apparently brutal in demanding that employees strive to achieve his super-elastic goals. “‘We can’t do that’ is not in SpaceX’s lexicon,” she likes to intone. “I’m not a tech developer, but it’s my job to figure out how to do all these crazy things, and if you think ‘there’s no way we’re doing that,’ you zip it, you think about it, and you find ways to get it done.”

In fact, Shotwell mirrors the boss’s wishes by running just about the most demanding workplace on earth. “One year at SpaceX is like 10 anywhere else. There’s no boundary between work and life outside of work,” Branden Spikes, SpaceX’s CIO for nearly 10 years, told Fortune. Musk has said that if 10% of employees aren’t leaving each year, his companies aren’t running at maximum efficiency.

Shotwell echoes that approach, in a nicer way. “We ‘counsel out’ about 10% of employees each year,” she says. “If you don’t like continuous feedback, if you don’t like running a marathon, if you want to walk a marathon, you don’t want to work at SpaceX.”

Shotwell’s behind-the-scenes, find-the-dollars pragmatism allowed SpaceX to take daredevil chances that delivered. But now, Shotwell’s the steward of a public company, and she’s showing her pragmatism by publicly tempering some of her boss’s more outrageous forecasts. Musk predicts in typical style that Starlink will multiply its broadband universe to 100,000 satellites in five years. In a good sign of caution, Shotwell puts the number at 12,000 to 15,000, keeping in mind that its new V3 models are far more powerful than their predecessors.

SpaceX now comprises three main businesses: “Space,” or the launch arm; the Starlink satellite franchise plus the fledgling Starlink Mobile, grouped as “Connectivity” in its financial reports; and AI, now called Super Intelligence (SI), comprising terrestrial data campuses, inherited from xAI, and the forthcoming Starmind orbital AI data centers, which unite xAI’s expertise with Starship’s capacity to launch giant satellites that bring compute to space.

In broadband satellite and launch, Musk and Shotwell have built one of the deepest moats in tech. SpaceX’s Space segment is “a decade-plus ahead of any competitor,” Julie Zhu, an analyst at MoffettNathanson, wrote in a recent report. Starlink accounts for three-quarters of all the broadband birds in orbit, and last year SpaceX flew 165 orbital missions, 85% of the U.S. and half the world total.

SpaceX is also pushing hard in terrestrial data centers. The former xAI built the first phase of a giant facility called Colossus 1 in just 120 days in 2024; the campus now covers 200 acres in the Memphis area, and its Colossus 2 claims the title of the world’s largest data center. Led by the Colossus expansion, SpaceX vows to grow its capacity more than fourfold to 13 gigawatts by the close of next year, adding in around a year and a half what Google built in its entire existence.

Colossus was first built primarily to run the Grok chatbot, which never caught the leader group of Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini. But Musk had shrewdly filled the facilities with Nvidia GPUs and other advanced chips now in short supply, and starting in May, he and Shotwell began leasing space to rivals famished for capacity. Deals with Google, Anthropic, Reflection AI and a fourth, undisclosed major player generate an incredible $3.4 billion a month in revenue. Renters can cancel at the end of a 90-day period, which helps explain the extremely high rates, but if the AI capex boom continues, the earth-based campuses should prove strongly profitable for years. Zhu predicts that the terrestrial group will supply the highest revenues of the four sectors, reaching $102 billion by 2031, 40% of the SpaceX total.

Musk and Shotwell, however, are counting on a totally unproven horizon in AI as the primary force in making SpaceX the world’s biggest and most profitable enterprise in a matter of years. At first look—and the way the pair characterize them—orbital AI data centers look far superior to their terrestrial counterparts, at least once SpaceX tames the launching costs, always a top strength.

Shotwell sketches that celestial image just as enthusiastically as her boss. During a CNBC interview in June, she argued that “the most efficient place for AI compute is in space,” and backed that “space is better” scenario at the All-In Summit tech conference in mid-September. On a panel, she cited that terrestrial campuses face long lag times for permits, licensing, and power supplies, and that land costs are enormous, avowing that “when someone finds out supercompute is going in, real estate goes from $3,000 to $180,000 an acre.” Yet, she added, “People need compute now.” Orbital centers will immensely speed the process, she maintained. “The real estate in space is infinite. And it’s free,” declared Shotwell; she also stressed that SpaceX can supply everything in house from the giant new Starship that will carry the loads to custom-manufacturing for the AI birds, which she says are “much simpler” than the V3 satellites. She even did something seldom witnessed at SpaceX: advanced the timing, forecasting that the AI satellites will fly into low-earth orbit next year, up from the pre-IPO target of 2028.

Besides providing the compute much quicker, the AI data centers, Shotwell and Musk argue, should be far cheaper. The reason: Power and cooling account for as much as 70% of a data center’s operating costs, and Musk and Shotwell argue correctly that plants in orbit pay nothing in direct expense for electricity or for keeping chips at an optimal temperature. “Deep space is the coldest thing out there,” Shotwell said at the All-In event. Yet all major studies now show that with current technology, orbital centers would cost a lot more all-in than the big boxes in Loudoun County, Va., or outside Memphis. Andrew McCalip, head of research at Varda Space Industries, reckons that running a 1 GW facility in orbit would cost $51.1 billion for the first five years, against $15.9 billion for the terrestrial equivalent.

Put simply, orbital centers trade much lower operating costs for far higher upfront expense for equipment, the heavy charges for lifting it into space, and most of all, a shorter life. Heating and cooling in space also aren’t “free.” Space has no atmosphere, so chips can’t be cooled by air or water as on earth; a modest-sized 100 MW data center requires a cluster of some 700 satellites, each carrying big radiators and solar panels. Each would feature 1,200-square-foot radiators, equal in size to one-and-a-half pickleball courts.

A major reason for the three-to-one cost differential: lifting each unit, with its 231-foot wingspan, into orbit. Today, SpaceX estimates its launch costs at around $2,700 per kg, and Shotwell and Musk pledge to crush that number to under $200 in a couple of years, on the way to below $100. Their big ace, besides Starship, is the Louisiana site that will be the world’s largest spaceport. By 2035, Adam Jonas of Morgan Stanley predicts, seven flights a day—and likely far more—will depart on Starship from four sites, most of the launches from the Louisiana coast. But slaying the launch-cost dragon isn’t enough, according to experts Fortune interviewed. Radiation gradually degrades the radiators and solar panels, causing them to lose potency over time. Earthbound facilities experience annualized failure rates of 3% to 5% for their equipment, but mechanics can replace the faulty units in minutes. No robot repair crews exist in space, and building them would hugely add to costs. The chips must also be space-hardened, which Nvidia is developing specifically for SpaceX, while its Terafab joint venture with Intel and Tesla works on custom orbital semiconductors.

Data centers in space also have an estimated life of just five years, while on earth the buildings, cooling, and power systems function far longer. That, plus gradually declining power and no way to fix parts gone bad, will make it extremely tough for orbital centers to compete with the giant campuses on earth.

Says a top executive in the data center industry, “My overall conclusion is that these are very difficult technical challenges. I just don’t see the problem it’s solving. … If you can develop chips that run far hotter for space and produce more power, why not use them on earth? We have a power grid on earth.”

But this titan also cautions, “Elon’s record is significant. I’m not sure I’d bet for it, but I’m also not ready to bet against it.” Several sources interviewed by Fortune believe that orbital data centers’ best prospects are as “escape valves” that offer needed capacity if the backlash against terrestrial campuses takes hold long-term. That’s conceivable, but hardly a highly investable scenario.

Technical issues pose a big barrier, and so does money. Overall, Wall Street was projecting the biggest capex blowout in corporate history before the Q2 surprise and announcement of the epic project in Louisiana. Jonas is typical among the analysts in positing that SpaceX won’t begin to see significant sales from Musk’s brainchild until at least 2032. Though Morgan Stanley posits that the campaign will eventually be a big winner, the timeline to getting there spotlights the difficulty. It predicts that SpaceX will burn cash through 2030, and require $390 billion in debt financing through that date to help fund its gigantic capex spend over the next eight to nine years.

As Morgan Stanley and other banks highlight, SpaceX can dial back on capex if the prospects for AI in space start looking dim. But as Shotwell acknowledges, SpaceX almost never delivers on time, and for years to come it may wrestle with the new technologies needed to make orbital compute profitable, without a clear line of sight to when, or if, that will happen. Meanwhile, heavy spending subsidized by Starlink could hammer overall earnings, and a share price elevated largely by great expectations for SpaceX’s galaxies of compute in low-earth orbit.

Shotwell has spent two decades proving the skeptics wrong, over and over. This time she’s facing engineering hurdles that even executives unwilling to bet against Musk call very difficult, at a price tag in capex that Wall Street already rates as the biggest in the annals of big business. If anyone can find the money in Musk’s latest moonshot, it’s Shotwell. The harder question for SpaceX shareholders is what happens if he insists on chasing a dream and, for once, she can’t stop him.

Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune, covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

#5296. AI Is Accelerating Software Development — But Businesses Need a Better Way to Measure the Quality of What They Ship

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI-assisted development has quietly made the metrics boards rely on unreliable.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

Two major datasets show how far the dashboard has drifted from reality:

On a typical board dashboard, the throughput gains appear as headline numbers while the instability sits in a footnote. A director reading deployment frequency would see an organization getting faster, with no view of the review process thinning out underneath it.

DORA has acknowledged the gap. Its researchers introduced deployment rework rate, the proportion of deployments that are unplanned fixes, as a fifth measure in 2024. DORA’s Nathen Harvey said on DX’s Engineering Enablement podcast that the four keys aren’t sufficient on their own for understanding AI’s impact.

Rework rate is worth tracking, but it records the fix only after a customer has already hit the bug. It can’t warn you before a release.

Code coverage reports how much of a codebase some test executed. It says nothing about whether that test checked an outcome a customer cares about, and AI-generated test suites can push coverage up without improving that second question.

A suite can touch every branch of a checkout service and still never confirm that a customer paying in a second currency gets charged the right amount.

You build verification coverage from the customer side. Product, engineering and finance agree on the journeys that make or lose money: signup, checkout, the core action the product exists for and the permission flows enterprise buyers probe during procurement.

Each journey gets an expected outcome written in business terms, such as an order confirmed at the correct price or an invited user landing with the right role. For each release, the team records how many of those journeys it ran end to end on the release candidate, in real browsers and devices, and how many produced that outcome.

A CFO can read the result without a glossary: something like “47 of 52 revenue-critical journeys verified before release.” Because your team measures it before anything ships, it should move ahead of rework rate and change failure rate, which register problems only after customers find them.

Part of the pressure comes from outside engineering. Cyber underwriters have started asking CFOs how they are managing AI risk.

Directors who signed off on AI tooling budgets will also start asking what the spend bought besides volume. A rising deployment count tells them the team ships more often. Verification coverage tells them whether the product customers pay for still works.

Most teams can produce a first figure within a quarter by following four steps:

Agentic test automation platforms such as KaneAI now let teams run these journeys against the rendered product on every release candidate.

DORA metrics still belong on the dashboard, because they tell you how fast and how steadily your organization delivers. Add verification coverage beside them in your next monthly report, and protect it from the pressure every board metric attracts.

A team under pressure can raise its score by shortening the journey list. Require product and finance sign-off before anyone changes it, and show the list size next to the ratio.

Include the failure cases customers hit, such as a declined card or an expired session, because a journey verified only on its happy path tells the board less than the number suggests.

Expect the score to sit below 100%, and tell directors which journeys failed and why. When they ask what AI has changed, you can show them how much of what shipped was verified to work.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

#5295. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5294. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

For a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

By recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”

Seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

It seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

By then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”

That job falls to the new Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t plan on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

#5293. Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:30 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”

#5292. 5 Powerful Lessons Leaders Can Learn From People Who Pay It Forward

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Five leadership lessons on measuring the long-term value of investing in people.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.

While the research is exploratory and cannot establish cause and effect, it raises questions that extend well beyond philanthropy. Every organization invests in people, yet few measure what those investments make possible over a lifetime. Here are five lessons I believe leaders can take from our experience.

The paper introduces a measure called the William Louey Effect: the difference between the path a scholar actually followed and the one that might reasonably have been expected given their starting circumstances. The name matters less than the question behind it: compared with what?

Businesses regularly celebrate employees who complete leadership programs and subsequently earn promotions. But would those employees have succeeded without the training? A talented person who was already destined to thrive tells us relatively little about the program. Someone whose trajectory genuinely changed tells us considerably more.

Leaders should examine starting circumstances, not simply final achievements. Otherwise, they risk rewarding programs for identifying talent rather than developing it.

One of our paper’s most striking findings is also among its most uncertain. It estimates that parental income is approximately 46% less predictive of our scholars’ adult earnings than it is nationally in China, comparing coefficients of 0.27 and 0.50. But that estimate draws on income ranges reported by roughly 10 people, all originally selected for academic promise. Some of the difference might have existed without our support.

The same problem affects corporate high-potential programs. When participants outperform their peers, how much credit belongs to the program, and how much to the selection process? Good measurement requires intellectual humility. Leaders should distinguish between outcomes they observe and impact they can reasonably attribute to their intervention. Acknowledging uncertainty does not weaken a success story. It makes the conclusions more credible.

From the beginning, I encouraged scholars to pay their opportunities forward when they felt ready, whether through money, knowledge or time. I never wanted that expectation to become a condition of receiving support. The paper calls this voluntary reciprocity: giving that emerges from gratitude and personal conviction rather than contractual obligation.

Organizations often seek loyalty through retention bonuses, repayment clauses and restrictive agreements. Such mechanisms can serve legitimate purposes, but they cannot manufacture genuine commitment. Some of our earliest scholars independently established and funded a scholarship for Chinese students at Oxford. We did not require them to do so, because when people feel trusted rather than indebted, they have the freedom to turn an opportunity they received into something of their own.

Generosity becomes more powerful when people can see what it looks like. Several scholars who established the Oxford scholarship also mentor its recipients, offering guidance similar to the support they once received. They are passing forward not only financial resources, but a way of treating people.

The leadership lesson is practical. If you want employees to mentor colleagues, share knowledge and create opportunities, make those expectations visible through your own behavior. Take time to advise younger employees, introduce promising people to contacts who can help them, and continue supporting colleagues even when there is no immediate benefit to you. Then give others the freedom to contribute in their own ways.

A culture of generosity cannot be built through instructions alone. It grows when people repeatedly experience the behavior their leaders advocate.

We have never asked a scholar to repay their scholarship. Instead, many have supported relatives, mentored students or helped others pursue opportunities. One former scholar described the experience as bringing philanthropy forward by a generation. For business leaders, this suggests a broader definition of return on investment.

Consider an employee who leaves your company and becomes an exceptional manager elsewhere, or a former trainee who mentors people you will never meet. Your organization may receive no direct financial benefit, yet its investment continues producing value. Traditional performance dashboards rarely capture that contribution.

Our paper argues that measuring educational outcomes only at graduation or the first job can overlook changes that emerge much later, including leadership, entrepreneurship and upward mobility. The same applies to professional development. A program evaluated after 12 months may reveal little about the influence its participants eventually have on others. Leaders should consider staying connected with former employees and tracking how their contributions evolve, without treating their subsequent achievements as corporate property.

The Foundation offers its framework as a starting point, not a definitive answer. We hope other scholarship providers and universities will test it with larger groups and more rigorous comparisons. Business leaders need not adopt our terminology to apply the underlying principle.

When deciding whether an investment in people has succeeded, ask two questions: What did this person achieve, and what did they subsequently make possible for others? The second is harder to measure, and its benefits may never return directly to the organization that made the investment. But three decades after founding the Foundation, I have come to believe it may be the more important question.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.
