#5291. Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office.

In hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press.

Both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games, meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

Like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’ young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

The opening-weekend audience bears out the split. Women made up 67% of ticket buyers and 74% were between 18 and 34, according to the AP. Lionsgate studied the risks of opening against GTA from the earliest stage of dating the film and concluded the two could coexist.

While the Mature-rated GTA VI may have kept men of a certain age glued to their consoles this weekend, the PG-13 Sunrise on the Reaping held onto the core Hunger Games crowd: young women, along with teens too young to play the game.

That base may also have come out of thirst for a big-screen, four-quadrant blockbuster. This fall has been a sleepy season for PG-13 action movies, with dramas, documentaries, and R-rated fare dominating the box office and the zeitgeist. Audiences liked what they found: the film earned an A- CinemaScore, up from the B+ that greeted Songbirds & Snakes.

Overall, the weekend was a surprisingly strong one for theaters. Total domestic grosses topped $160 million, nearly double the prior weekend, though still about 10% below the same frame last year, when Wicked: For Good opened.

Sunrise on the Reaping accounted for most of that. Behind it on the weekend chart came I Play Rocky with $9.3 million in its first weekend of wide release, Ebenezer at $7.7 million, and The Cat in the Hat at $6.9 million. You Can See Everything is still hanging in the top 10, adding another $2.5 million.

These titles are diverse, but most target an audience different from GTA VI. Beyond The Hunger Games locking up young women, I Play Rocky is for the boomer dads and The Cat in the Hat is for kids.

None of it came close to GTA VI. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, says the game’s day-one retail sales, including preorders, reached $3.79 billion worldwide, more than 20 times the weekend’s entire domestic box office.

Still, Hollywood held its own heading into Thanksgiving week, suggesting that with the right strategy, audiences will still show up for the movies, and that GTA VI may not dominate every corner of the entertainment economy this season. The next test comes this weekend, when Sunrise on the Reaping faces a crowded holiday slate that includes Disney’s animated Hexed.

#5290. So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.

The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

“It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.”

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

A decisive close above the 200-day MA would signal trend improvement, opening paths toward $3,000–$4,000+ in a constructive environment, though percentage gains from current levels would likely trail more volatile peers.

Analyst scenarios often show wider upside ranges for SOL relative to current levels compared with ETH. Ethereum offers a more stable institutional foundation and could post solid absolute returns on successful upgrades and RWA growth, but its larger size typically compresses percentage upside.

Both face risks: macro headwinds, execution delays, competition, and residual network reliability questions for Solana. Crypto markets remain highly uncertain; past performance and roadmaps are not guarantees.

Investors should weigh risk tolerance carefully. In a constructive 2027 backdrop, Solana’s combination of technical momentum potential and upcoming catalysts gives it the edge for the strongest relative gains.

#5288. As AI Takes on More Work, a Leader’s Responsibility Only Grows. Here’s Why.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The pace of change is accelerating, and AI is reshaping how businesses work. But some things cannot be delegated to machines.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a new generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

We have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

The defining feature of our time is the exponential development of technology. Today, we are no longer talking simply about digitalization, but about the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence. AI is ceasing to be a standalone tool and is beginning to shape the environment in which businesses operate. It accelerates analysis, automates processes, changes consumer expectations and reduces the cost of many operations.

But as opportunities grow, so does human responsibility.

In the past, a company could operate for years based on a strategy chosen once and then followed consistently. Today, almost every change becomes a separate project: introducing artificial intelligence, modifying a product, restructuring sales channels or adapting to new customer habits. Entrepreneurs are no longer simply making decisions; they are constantly managing change.

Uncertainty is increasingly becoming the environment in which businesses are built. The question for every entrepreneur is whether they can make decisions and take action under such conditions.

I often say that entrepreneurship is not so much a profession as a state of mind. Education, planning and capital all help, but entrepreneurs must act with incomplete information, adapt, overcome setbacks and maintain the emotional balance required to lead others.

This is precisely why emotional intelligence matters so much. Strong analysts can be hired, but a leader must personally learn to manage their own reactions, understand others and communicate convincingly in stressful situations.

A team takes its cues from its leader. If the leader freezes, the organization slows down. If they act recklessly, it risks losing discipline. The challenge is to remain calm without becoming passive, and optimistic without ignoring risks.

Persistence is equally important: that inner drive that keeps you working until you achieve the desired result. At the same time, the tools and the route may change. It is important not to confuse persistence with stubbornness, or activity with actual progress.

The paradox is that as AI takes over more routine tasks, the responsibility of leaders continues to grow. It is the human being who determines the direction of development, builds the team and assesses strategic risks. The ability to understand what is happening and adapt more quickly is therefore becoming a key competitive advantage.

A leader can only step away from the controls when there are people around them capable of taking over. This makes one of the most important resources available to any leader the ability to build a strong team, establish trust with partners and delegate authority.

But there is a question that I believe is far more important than efficiency.

We talk far too often about how to outperform competitors, increase market capitalization or scale a business. Almost never do we ask ourselves a different question: What is the ultimate purpose of being human?

You can defeat your competitors, build the largest company and achieve extraordinary results. Yet none of these things guarantees what matters most: a happy life.

Most people define their goals in terms of achievements. Almost nobody says: My primary goal is to build the happiest possible life for myself. Yet this is precisely the goal that determines the value of all other achievements!

Inner exhaustion is not always simply a matter of how much work we do. If the lifestyle we have chosen consistently leads to it, we should ask ourselves what goals we are pursuing. Perhaps something needs to change.

So perhaps the most useful advice for entrepreneurs today is surprisingly simple: Start by understanding yourself. Understand your genuine emotional needs, strengths, natural abilities and limitations. Do not try to become someone you are not. Do not build a career that goes against your own nature.

People generally enjoy doing things they are good at. And they tend to become good at things they genuinely enjoy doing. When these two things coincide, the likelihood of success increases significantly.

This applies beyond business. Even philanthropy, traditionally regarded as an exclusively altruistic activity, naturally benefits the person who gives as well. The opportunity to share knowledge, help others and see the results of one’s actions all generate positive emotions. There is nothing wrong with that. It is simply human nature.

In general, many things become easier to understand when viewed through the lens of biology rather than conventional abstractions. Our emotions, motivation and sense of fulfillment have a very real physiological basis. Relationships with other people, meaningful work, the environment in which we live, our health and our ability to take pleasure in our own achievements — these are the elements that combine to create a sense of well-being.

Happiness, therefore, is neither a matter of luck nor a state of constant euphoria. It is a dynamic balance between the emotions a person genuinely needs and the states they experience at any given moment. This balance cannot be found once and preserved forever. It must be maintained continuously, with adjustments to our lives as the world around us changes.

And perhaps this is one of the greatest challenges of the age of artificial intelligence.

Machines may become increasingly capable of analyzing data, writing code, creating content, automating processes and helping us make decisions. But help with a decision is not the same as responsibility for it. The question of why we are in business and what kind of life we want to live remains ours to answer.

That is why a leader’s true competitive advantage lies not only in the ability to use AI, but also in the ability to remain the author of their own life.

Technology may change the rules of the game many times over. The pace of change may accelerate, and artificial intelligence may take over a significant share of intellectual work. But responsibility for our own decisions, our own happiness and our own path will remain with us.

And perhaps this is the most valuable skill a leader can possess today: the ability to maintain inner strength and remain the author of their own life, even as the world around them changes faster than ever before.

Over the past few years, entrepreneurs have been living in a state of constant mobilization. First came the pandemic, followed by geopolitical instability, shifting markets, the emergence of artificial intelligence and a new generation of technology-driven competitors.

After several years of running this marathon, it might seem that we should finally be able to catch our breath. Yet it is precisely now that we are beginning to realize that the pace of change is only accelerating.

We have become accustomed to looking for ways to manage stress: exercise, saunas, digital detoxes and meditation. But perhaps the problem is not simply how much time we spend resting. Perhaps the pace of change itself has fundamentally shifted.

#5286. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:02 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:56 am

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

#5285. RBC Signals brings in $10M investment to expand strategic frontiers for satellite services

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

#5284. An SEO Expert’s 3 Tactics for Getting Your Business Found Beyond Google

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Discover three practical strategies to help your business get found beyond Google through AI search, LinkedIn and brand mentions.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For years, getting found online meant getting found on Google. Businesses researched keywords, optimized their websites and built backlinks to attract potential customers.

Those things still matter. But today, someone might discover a business through ChatGPT, a LinkedIn post or a recommendation from someone they trust, without ever typing a query into Google.

As an AI and SEO specialist running Create & Grow, a digital marketing agency, I’ve learned that many of the principles behind effective SEO work just as well beyond search engines. You need to understand what people are looking for, give them a reason to pay attention and build enough authority for them to trust you.

Here’s how I’ve applied those principles to client campaigns and my own business.

Keyword research tells you what people search for, but it doesn’t always reveal how they describe their problems.

According to Salesforce’s State of the Connected Customer report, 73% of customers expect companies to understand their unique needs and expectations. To do that, businesses need to listen to customers, not just study search volumes.

I saw this firsthand while working with a client in the invoicing software industry.

Instead of relying exclusively on keyword tools, we analyzed the client’s support tickets, sales calls, live chats, customer reviews and internal search data. We wanted to understand how business owners described the problems that made them look for invoicing software in the first place.

They weren’t necessarily using technical phrases like “accounts receivable automation.” They talked about chasing late payments, making mistakes on invoices, wasting hours on repetitive tasks and struggling to predict cash flow.

That distinction shaped our strategy. Rather than promoting the software through generic accounting terminology, we focused on connecting the client’s brand to the specific problems its customers wanted to solve.

We built those associations through digital PR, guest articles, LinkedIn posts, company page optimization and relevant niche edits on third-party websites. We also prioritized branded links and mentions instead of focusing exclusively on keyword-rich backlinks.

Our outreach campaign generated a mix of dofollow and nofollow backlinks, as well as unlinked brand mentions. Our goal wasn’t simply to earn backlinks. We wanted the client’s brand to appear consistently in conversations about the problems its software addressed.

This matters beyond traditional search. Someone might ask ChatGPT, “What software can help me stop chasing unpaid invoices?” When credible websites repeatedly connect a brand with that problem, AI systems have more relevant context about what the company offers.

That doesn’t guarantee a recommendation, but it makes the brand’s positioning clearer to both AI tools and potential customers.

We applied the same thinking to the client’s website. We created customer case studies showing how the invoicing software solved real problems and made pricing publicly available so potential buyers could evaluate the product more easily. Both changes also made commercially useful information accessible to AI search tools.

After six months, the client’s organic traffic increased by almost 25%, ranking keywords grew by 31%, and keywords in Google’s Top 10 increased by 39%. Most importantly, organic demo requests rose by 44%.

Those results came from our combined SEO and brand-building efforts, not one isolated tactic. We also deliberately prioritized commercial intent over traffic volume. As AI-generated answers increasingly satisfy informational searches, attracting people actively evaluating invoicing solutions matters more than ranking for every broad accounting question.

The same principle applies when you’re trying to get someone else’s attention. Before asking for anything, understand what that person might actually find valuable.

I put this into practice recently when I wanted to publish guest articles on a few high-authority websites.

Most guest-post outreach starts with a predictable request: “Do you accept guest contributions?” I wanted my message to stand out by showing editors exactly what they could gain from working with me.

So I researched relevant websites and contacted their editors and marketing managers with examples of articles I’d already published. These weren’t generic pieces that anyone could produce with an AI writing tool. They combined firsthand experience from real SEO campaigns, original insights, practical examples, research and relevant statistics.

I also made sure the articles were properly optimized for search, but the real selling point was the value they delivered to readers.

Then I showed the results. I included evidence of the organic traffic those articles attracted, the keywords they ranked for on Google and the citations and brand mentions they earned in AI-generated answers.

In other words, I wasn’t asking editors to imagine what I could deliver. I was showing them a finished example of the quality, expertise and measurable value I could bring to their websites.

Only then did I make my offer: “Would you like me to create something like this for your website, for free?”

That’s a very different proposition from asking someone for a backlink or a guest-post opportunity. The editor gets a thoroughly researched, experience-driven article that can attract relevant visitors and strengthen the website’s authority. I get an opportunity to demonstrate my expertise to a new audience.

To reach people outside my existing network, I used LinkedIn Premium All-in-One, which includes InMail messaging. I didn’t need all 30 monthly InMail credits. Roughly 10 carefully targeted messages generated three client inquiries and one paying customer.

Some recipients became interested in my SEO consulting, content strategy and outreach services after seeing the work I could do. One company ultimately hired me to improve its outreach process and develop stronger pitches.

What’s interesting is that I hadn’t approached these people to sell SEO services. I led with proof of what I could create for them, made an offer that was genuinely useful and let the business conversation develop naturally.

That’s why I prefer carefully researched outreach over sending hundreds of generic messages. The objective isn’t to contact as many people as possible. It’s to make your offer so relevant and valuable that the recipient has a compelling reason to respond.

One well-researched message can open a door. But consistently useful content can make people familiar with your work long before you ever contact them.

That’s why I treat LinkedIn content planning much like SEO research. Before publishing, I study competing digital marketing agencies: their websites, LinkedIn posts and how they position their expertise. I look at which topics generate engagement, what questions their audiences ask and where their content leaves room for a better answer.

I use those insights to plan content for my personal LinkedIn profile. Some posts share practical lessons about SEO, AI search and digital marketing, often drawn from my own campaigns. Others are deliberately more relaxed and humorous.

The professional posts show people how I solve problems. The humorous ones make my content more relatable and give people another reason to engage. I don’t expect every post to generate a lead, and I certainly don’t want every post to read like a sales pitch.

Instead, I want people to recognize my work over time. And that has become a reliable source of conversations and client opportunities.

Some people reach out through LinkedIn messages after reading my posts. Others start conversations in the comments. I’ve also met people at conferences who tell me they’ve followed my content for years. We might talk about SEO, exchange ideas and stay in touch. Sometimes, months later, they contact me about a project and become clients.

By then, I don’t need to start by explaining who I am or convincing them that I understand SEO. They’ve already seen how I think, what I know and the results I share.

That matters because B2B buyers often develop preferences before contacting a provider. According to 6sense‘s 2025 B2B Buyer Experience Report, in 77% of B2B purchases studied, buyers ended up choosing the company they already preferred before their first sales conversation.

My experience illustrates why that matters in practice: Someone who has followed your work for a long time may already trust your expertise when they finally need your services.

The next step is making sure that first interaction doesn’t become the last. On LinkedIn, that might mean giving readers a reason to follow your personal profile or company page. Outside LinkedIn, an email newsletter can help you stay connected with website visitors. You could even build a private Slack community where people in your industry exchange ideas, ask questions and learn from one another.

Whatever channel you choose, the principle is the same: Offer enough value that people want to stay connected. Then keep showing up with content worth their attention.

SEO taught me to understand what customers need, pay attention to the competition and build authority through useful content. Those principles now help me get discovered through AI tools, LinkedIn and relationships that start well before a sales conversation.

You don’t need to abandon Google or be active on every platform. Start by speaking your customers’ language, approaching new contacts with something valuable and creating content that gives people a reason to keep following your work.

If you’re ready to make your business easier to find and harder to forget, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to see which ones fit your strategy.

Getting discovered creates the opportunity. Being remembered and trusted is what turns that opportunity into business.

For years, getting found online meant getting found on Google. Businesses researched keywords, optimized their websites and built backlinks to attract potential customers.

Those things still matter. But today, someone might discover a business through ChatGPT, a LinkedIn post or a recommendation from someone they trust, without ever typing a query into Google.

As an AI and SEO specialist running Create & Grow, a digital marketing agency, I’ve learned that many of the principles behind effective SEO work just as well beyond search engines. You need to understand what people are looking for, give them a reason to pay attention and build enough authority for them to trust you.

#5282. John Deere acquires Orchard Robotics, an AI farming startup with Seattle ties

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am

Orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

The startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

“Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu said in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round announced in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

#5281. StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

StepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

StepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

The company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#5280. The 10 Best Gifts for Entrepreneurs to Buy During Black Friday Week

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Struggling to know what to get for the entrepreneurs and small business owners in your life? Here’s the answer.

The store is finally quiet. Even though the last customer has left, the owner’s laptop is still open, and their to-do list is overwhelmingly long. There’s still one more email to answer, one more thing to do.

Buying a gift for that person, the small business owner or entrepreneur with a lot on their plate, can be surprisingly difficult. Another motivational mug might elicit a smile, but it will probably not make Monday easier. A more thoughtful choice is something that fits the way they actually work.

That is the thinking behind these 10 gift ideas. Rather than treating every entrepreneur as a startup founder glued to a laptop, this list considers several kinds of working days. There are options for people building a business from the kitchen table.

Black Friday adds another consideration. Is a useful gift genuinely available for less? Amazon’s current sale coverage includes discounts on headphones, microphones, computer accessories and other work-friendly technology.

The right choice still depends on the recipient. The most meaningful gift shows that you have noticed the person behind the business.

Here are the 10 best gifts for entrepreneurs.

Square Terminal: For the business owner ready to simplify checkout

Square Terminal combines sales, card payments and receipt-printing in one device. It’s a practical gift candidate for a store owner who wants to bundle those tasks together. Its built-in battery also allows cordless use around the business rather than keeping every transaction tied to one spot. Before ordering, ask if the recipient wants to use Square and if this terminal fits their existing setup. This product is currently over 10% off, making the final price $265.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite, 16GB: For the entrepreneur who has time to read

This Kindle Paperwhite has a seven-inch glare-free display, 16GB of storage and battery life of up to 12 weeks. For an entrepreneur, this gift could allow them to read a biography on a flight, return to a novel after closing the shop or finally start the book a friend recommended. Its appeal is especially clear for someone who already reads digitally but would appreciate a separate reading device. Think twice before buying if the person is devoted to paper books or has never expressed an interest in e-readers. This Kindle is $70 off for Black Friday, making it $130 total.

reMarkable Paper Pro bundle with Marker Plus and black leather Book Folio: For the handwritten thinker

Some entrepreneurs think best by writing things out. They sketch a plan or rewrite a sentence until the argument becomes clear. The reMarkable Paper Pro is aimed at that style of work, with an 11.8-inch color display and adjustable reading light. It is a color e-ink paper tablet that doubles as a digital notebook for writing and drawing. The requested package includes the Marker Plus pen and black leather Book Folio. As a gift, it makes the most sense for someone whose working day already involves handwritten notes, like a founder mapping a new service. This package is $100 off for Black Friday, making the final price about $700.

Bose QuietComfort Bluetooth Headphones: For the entrepreneur looking for some peace and quiet

Bose QuietComfort headphones offer active noise cancellation, a built-in microphone and up to 24 hours of playback. That makes them a thoughtful choice for someone who regularly works around other people. The headphones also allow the recipient to use them for music or listening to podcasts or e-books during time off. Make sure to consider whether the recipient mentioned wanting over-ear headphones and if they already wear a pair throughout the day. Only some colors have the Black Friday discount, which is 53%, or $190 off, for a final price of $169.

Gloryang 668BT thermal shipping-label printer: For the seller packing orders at home

The Gloryang 668BT prints standard 4-by-6-inch shipping labels and supports label widths from one to 4.4 inches. Its Bluetooth and USB connections support use with phones, tablets and computers. This is a useful device for a small shop owner who has said that their labeling process needs improvement. It’s also compact and is 25% off for Black Friday, for a final price of $43.

Anker Laptop Power Bank: For the entrepreneur who always needs a charger

Their laptop battery runs out of charge just as a client meeting begins, and their phone is nearly dead too. A business owner who works across shared spaces and cafes could find a portable charger to be a thoughtful gift. This charger is a strong gift for a consultant or founder who regularly carries several devices. A Black Friday deal brings the price of this charger below $100, at 32% off, which is a 90-day low price. It costs about $91.

Shure SM7B dynamic vocal microphone: For the owner building a podcast

This gift is for a business owner who records interviews, lessons or a podcast. The Shure SM7B is a dynamic vocal microphone designed for uses including podcasting, broadcast and recording. Its pickup pattern focuses on sound in front of the microphone. The SM7B uses an XLR connection rather than a direct USB connection; the XLR is better for sound quality. The microphone is $70 off for Black Friday, bringing its price to $369 at the time of writing.

Apple Magic Mouse with USB-C: For the Apple user who wants a clean-looking accessory

Apple’s Magic Mouse is wireless and rechargeable. Its Multi-Touch surface supports gestures such as scrolling through documents and swiping between web pages. The USB-C version includes a charging cable, and Apple says its battery can last about a month or more between charges. This is a good gift for an entrepreneur who already likes Apple’s mouse design. The clean accessory is a safe option if the recipient currently uses a Magic Mouse and wants another for a second workspace. The white color is on sale for $20 off this Black Friday, making its price about $60.

Soundcore P30i noise-cancelling earbuds: For an affordable, useful everyday gift

The Soundcore P30i earbuds offer noise cancellation and a charging case that doubles as a phone stand. The product listing also advertises up to 45 hours of total playback. The phone-stand feature adds a small practical touch. Their size makes them a reasonable candidate for someone who prefers carrying earbuds rather than over-ear headphones. They are perfect for listening during a commute. The earbuds were originally listed for about $50 but are more than 50% off for Black Friday, bringing the price down to $24.

Soundcore Select 4 Go Bluetooth speaker: For making the workday a little more enjoyable

A small speaker can be a welcome addition to the hours spent working in a store or office. The Soundcore Select 4 Go is a compact Bluetooth speaker with a five-watt output. Its product listing advertises up to 20 hours of playback and an IP67 water- and dust-resistance rating. It is the ideal gift for an entrepreneur who likes having music nearby as they move between different working spaces. A Black Friday deal slashes the price to a 365-day low, making it $20 when it was originally $35.

#5279. October 22, 2019

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed plans for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” says one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too quickly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”

SoftBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one big reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”

Blueground, a six-year-old, New York-based startup providing turnkey flexible rental apartments, has raised $50 million in Series B funding, roughly six months after raising $20 million in Series A funding. WestCap Investment Partners and Prime Ventures co-led the round. More here.

Databricks, a six-year-old, San Francisco-based SaaS business that’s built on top of a bunch of open source tools, has raised a massive $400 million in Series F funding at a post-money valuation of $6.2 billion valuation. Today’s funding brings the total raised to almost a $900 million. Andreessen Horowitz led the round with new investors BlackRock,  T. Rowe Price Associates, and Tiger Global Management also participating. TechCrunch has more here.

IonQ, a four-year-old, College Park, Md.-based startup that uses charged particles suspended in a vacuum, as the basis for its hardware, has raised $55 million in funding. Samsung and Mubadala Capital co-led the round, joined by Amazon, GV, and New Enterprise Associates. Fortune has more here.

Aurora Insight, a three-year-old, Washington, D.C.-based startup that provides a “dynamic” global map of wireless connectivity that it built and monitors in real time using AI combined with data from sensors on satellites, vehicles, buildings, aircraft and other objects, has raised $18 million in Series A funding. Alsop Louie Partners and True Ventures co-led the round,  joined by Tippet Venture Partners, Rise of the Rest Seed Fund, Promus Ventures, Alumni Ventures Group, ValueStream Ventures, and Intellectus Partners. TechCrunch has more here.

Benevity, an 11-year-old, Calgary, Alberta-based company that makes corporate social responsibility and employee engagement software, has raised $30.5 million in Series C funding from General Atlantic and JMI Equity. More here. EV Connect, a 10-year-old, L.A.-based company that sells software to manage electric vehicle charging, has raised $12 million in a Series B round led by Mitsui & Co. and Ecosystem Integrity Fund. The company has raised $25 million to date. TechCrunch has more here.

Octave, a year-old, San Francisco-based tech-based behavioral health practice, has raised $11 million in Series A funding led by Greycroft, with participation from Obvious Ventures and earlier backers. The company has raised at least $14 million to date. Crunchbase News has more here.Signal AI, a six-year-old, London-based business intelligence and media monitoring startup, has raised $25 million in Series C funding. Redline Capital led the round, joined by MMC Ventures, GMG Ventures, and Hearst Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

AllWork, a 3.5-year-old, New York-based on-demand work platform that’s targeting large enterprise customers in need of temporary workers, has raised $3.8 million in seed funding from Great Oaks, Lightspeed Scout Fund, The Fund, Fernbrook, SmartHub, and numerous angel investors. More here.

Beem, a year-old, Boston-based CBD company that’s marketing its branded oils, protein bars, and a salve to athletes who may be looking for alternatives to chemically derived pain relievers and anti-inflammatories, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by Obvious Ventures. TechCrunch has more here.

Intrepida Bio, a newly launched, San Diego-based biotech focused on modulating innate immune systems, has raised $9.5 million from Sofinnova and Canaan Partners. FierceBiotech has more here.

LabGenius, a seven-year-old, London-based startup that’s applying AI and robotic automation to protein drug discovery, has raised $10 million in Series A funding. The round was led by Lux Capital and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Felicis Ventures, Inovia Capital, Air Street Capital and earlier investors, along with numerous notable individuals. TechCrunch has more here.

Margin Edge, a four-year-old, Falls Church, Va.-based maker of restaurant management software, has raised $5 million in Series A funding led by Osage Venture Partners, with participation from Good Company. More here.

Medinas, a two-year-old, Berkeley, Ca.-based company that helps healthcare organizations resell their surplus medical equipment and supplies, has raised $5 million in seed funding led by NFX. Additional investors in the round include Precursor Ventures, Sound Ventures, FJ Labs and Bryan Frist (of HCA Healthcare’s founding family). Crunchbase News has more here.

MediView XR, a two-year-old, Cleveland, Oh.-based medical device company working on a surgical navigation system that leverages augmented reality and spatial computing to provide surgeons with advanced visualization, has raised $4.5 million in seed funding. Backers include Inside View Investment,Plug and Play Ventures and Northwest Ohio Tech Fund. More here.

Reibus, a year-old, Atlanta, Ga.-based online marketplace for industrial materials, has raised $3.25 million in seed funding led by Bowery Capital, with participation from Initialized Capital and Stage 2 Capital. More here.

Marcelo Claure, the chief operating officer of SoftBank Group, will assume the position of executive chairman of the board of directors of WeWork when the company receives a planned $1.5 billion payment from SoftBank. TechCrunch has more here.

John Donahoe, the current president and CEO of ServiceNow, is taking over as the CEO and president of Nike in January, replacing Mark Parker who has been since 2006 and lived through numerous controversies over the years. Donahoe knows Nike well, having joined its board, where he will retain a seat, since 2014. In the meantime, Parker will become the company’s executive chairman and Bill McDermott, who abruptly resigned as the longtime CEO of SAP earlier this month for reasons that weren’t clear, is taking over as CEO of ServiceNow. The company’s shareholders apparently prefer Donahoe, who is also the chairman of PayPal and a former CEO of eBay, which he led from 2008 through 2015. At least, shares of ServiceNow dropped in price on the news.

Zaz Floreani has joined the Austin-based venture firm Next Coast Ventures as a principal. Floreani was most recently the VP of corporate development at the same-day delivery company Dropoff. More here.

Manuel Henriquez, founder and former CEO of Hercules Growth Technology Capital, and his wife Elizabeth have both pleaded guilty for their roles in the college admissions cheating scandal. She is to be sentenced Feb. 7 and her husband on March 5. The San Jose Mercury News has more here.

Why the Oscars, Emmys and Tonys are not ready for they and them.

A machine-learning system that’s betting the Astros will win the World Series (though our money is still on the Nats).

#5278. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.)

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on a deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and others aren’t built to process.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

Angela Gunn is a GRC consultant and vCISO with Ericius Security. She has worked in infosec and incident response roles for companies including Microsoft, HP and BAE Systems Applied Intelligence. Prior to working in the tech sector, she covered it as a journalist for publications including USA Today, PC Magazine, Computerworld, Yahoo! Internet Life and Seattle Weekly.
